Purpose of the Course
Digital transformation of work, project work and management
▪Two Major trends affecting the nature of work: 
▪Increasing importance of projects, multi-project management, and new 
approaches to project management, such as agile methods
▪Digital technologies in organizations and at the workplace continue to transform 
work practices, the coordination of work, and the division of labor
▪The project management parts of this course concern the theoretical 
foundation for the management of (IT) projects as one of the common 
organizational (IT) endeavors in practice.
▪Delving into the realm of digital work, the course introduces key aspects in 
modern work environments, including data-driven decision making, digital 
communication, and digital collaboration, as well as the introduction and use 
of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in workplace settings.
▪Two joint topics on agility and virtual (project) teams merge digital work and 
project management perspectives, equipping students with essential skills for 
navigating modern work environments.

Learning Objectives (1/3)
What you should take away from this course
▪Understand the specifics of communicating and collaborating digitally
▪Understand how to manage virtual teams successfully
▪Become acquainted with the impact of AI-based systems on today’s work
▪Scrutinize people analytics and algorithmic management as digital management 
practices
▪Understand how insights from data affect decision making
Benedikt Berger & Raimund Vogl | Introduction
14
Learning Objectives (2/3)
What you should take away from this course
▪Understand the notion of projects, as opposed to organisational routines (operations)
▪Understand the project life cycle and the project management process groups
▪Understand how to manage the project “magic triangle”: scope, schedule, and cost
▪Understand how to manage a project team and to communicate with internal and 
external project stakeholders
▪Understand how to monitor and manage quality and risks in projects
▪Understand how to manage documents in projects (knowledge management) as well as 
project portfolios (multi-project management)
Benedikt Berger & Raimund Vogl | Introduction

Learning Objectives (3/3)

▪Getting to know digital competencies and tools to manage your own work
▪Deepen knowledge on agile project management techniques
▪Improve project management skills by applying selected software tools
▪Practice how to solve business problems by applying your knowledge from the lectures
▪Train group work, presentation, and discussion skills in a scientific context

Course Format
Pooling of lectures and exercises
▪Lectures and exercises take place in-person
▪Tuesdays & Wednesdays, from 2.15 to 3.45 pm
▪Leo 1 lecture hall at Leonardo-Campus 10 (except for May 5th: S1 in the castle)
▪This course does not follow the typical “lecture precedes exercise” logic, 
which is why there is no dedicated lecture or exercise day.
▪Instead, we decided to pool lectures and exercises in topic clusters, 
alternating between project management, digital work, and joint parts                                           
▪Each part begins with a (series of) lecture(s) to introduce relevant concepts, 
theories, and methods
▪These lectures are followed by (a series of) different types of interactive 
exercises to apply, reflect, and deepen the previously gained knowledge
▪For a detailed overview of lectures and exercises, please see the schedule in 
this slide deck or on Learnweb.

Group Work Organization
Allocation mechanism
▪In each case study session, up to 6 groups present their case studies analyses. 
▪Therefore, students will be in one of ~24 groups. The groups will be of equal 
sizes. Accordingly, the group size depends on the overall number of students.
▪Groups will be built using the “Group Choice” mechanism on Learnweb. 
Everyone can register for their preferred case study topic on a first come, 
first served basis, allowing students to build their own groups.
▪Disclaimer: There is no guarantee that you will be assigned to a topic or group 
that you originally chose. We reserve the right to transfer students from one 
group to another if a group is of insufficient size.
Students must join a group on Learnweb
between Tuesday, April 14th, 5:00 pm and Monday, April 20th, 
11:59 pm.

Frequently Asked Questions
Some answers
Will the exam be in English?
Like the whole course, the examination sheet will be completely in English. 
You must write your answers in English (answers in German will not be graded)!
Where do I get the book that the PM part is based on?
The main text book for the project management parts is the Project 
Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) 6th Edition, which is available 
in the library (Leonardo-Campus 3).
Benedikt Berger & Raimund Vogl | Introduction

Frequently Asked Questions
Some answers
If I postpone the final exam, will I be able to transfer my points for the group 
assignments?
Yes, you can transfer your points for the continuous assessment in the summer 
term 2026 to any upcoming final examination!
How should the written report be structured?
You may structure your written report like a typical research paper 
(introduction / body / conclusion) or address the tasks individually.
Two important remarks:
1. Don’t plagiarise, we will check it! Find out more about “What Constitutes 
Plagiarism?”.
2. Cite properly using e.g. APA (American Psychological Association) style, 7th 
edition (citation software helps)!
3. Clearly mark the use of generative AI content (see UM FAQ on AI usage).

44
1.
Projects are temporary (definite beginning and end) endeavours 
undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.
2.
Projects have specific goals, budgets, and deadlines.
3.
Projects aim to move organisations from one state to another to 
achieve specific objectives.
▪Projects drive change in organisations.
▪Projects enable business value creation.
4.
Projects often exceed the boundaries of departments or organisations. 
They often involve a project team that is composed of experts from 
various disciplines.
5.
Projects are initiated by organisational leaders in response to factors 
acting upon their organisations (context): regulatory, legal, or social 
requirements; stakeholder requests or needs.

Project Stakeholders
Definition and aspects to consider
▪An individual, group, or organisation that may affect, be affected by, or 
perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity, or outcome of a 
project
▪May be internal or external to the project
▪May be actively or passively involved, or unaware of the project
▪May have a positive or negative impact on the project
▪May be positively or negatively impacted by the project
▪Aspects that are critical to project success:
▪Successful identification, analysis, and engagement of stakeholders
▪Effective management of stakeholder expectations from the project
▪Effective management of stakeholder participation throughout the project 
life cycle

Tools and Techniques: Critical Path Method (CPM)
▪Critical path
▪A sequence of activities, which add up to the longest overall project duration 
(=shortest time to complete project)
▪Slack
▪The amount of time that an activity can be delayed without changing the overall 
duration of the project
▪Every activity with a zero slack is on the critical path
▪Activities with minor slacks also need to be carefully looked at, because any delays 
in those activities could cause them to be on a new critical path
▪Critical Path Method (CPM)
▪Identifies the activities that are critical or essential for the project timely 
completion
▪Extends the Project Schedule Network Diagrams

▪Analogous estimating (top-down estimating)

Raimund Vogl | Project Schedule & Cost Management
Contingency and Management Reserve
Idea: To include buffers in the budget to account for cost uncertainty
▪Contingency Reserve: “known unknowns”
▪buffer for known risks with active response strategies
▪e.g., rework for some project deliverables could be anticipated, while the amount of this rework is not yet known
▪can be provided for a specific activity, for the whole project, or both
▪may be a percentage of the estimated cost, a fixed number, or developed by using quantitative analysis methods
▪may be used, reduced, or eliminated, once more precise information about the project becomes available
▪should be clearly identified in cost documentation is part of the cost baseline and the overall funding 
requirements for the project
▪Management Reserve: “unknown unknowns”
▪buffer that is reserved for unforeseen work that is within scope of the project
▪is not included in the cost baseline, but is part of the overall project budget and funding requirements
▪the used amount of management reserve is added to the cost baseline (once respective change to the cost 
baseline is approved)

Budget at completion, estimate at completion, and estimate to complete 
Budget At Completion (BAC) = Cost Baseline
▪The sum of all budgets established for the work to be performed (not management reserve!)
▪Total PV for the project
Estimate To Complete (ETC)
▪The expected cost to finish all the remaining project work: ETC = BAC – EV
▪(Alternatively, divide by CPI: ETC = (BAC-EV)/CPI to account for past performance)
Estimate At Completion (EAC) 
▪The expected total cost of completing all work
▪The sum of AC to date and ETC: EAC = AC + ETC = BAC + AC – EV
▪If it becomes obvious that the BAC is no longer viable, the project manager should consider 
the forecasted EAC

Introduction

The Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) method 
A foundational tool in TQM
▪An iterative management method used in organisations to facilitate the control and 
continual improvement of processes and products. PDCA is not just in TQM - ISO 
quality standards are also PDCA based.
▪Plan (drive, direct)
▪Assess a current process / product and develop a plan how it can be improved 
▪Do (deploy, support, participate)
▪Implement the developed plan and gather performance data
▪Check (review)
▪Evaluate the gathered data
▪Act (recognise, communicate, revise)
▪Decide based on the performed evaluation, whether the plan implemented in “Do” 
improves the prior standard, and, if yes, it becomes the new standard

Six Sigma
Introduction
▪A customer-focused continuous improvement strategy and discipline that aims 
at minimising defects and variability of outcomes and/or processes. 
▪Goal: to achieve a variation of 6σ (between upper and lower quality bounds), 
which equals 3.4 errors per million process executions (or a quality level of 
99,99966%) – virtually no errors!
▪Use of problem solving and statistical tools to improve business processes
▪The Six Sigma method acts as a foundation for further methods to improve 
organisational performance (e.g., Lean Six Sigma)
▪The Six Sigma method was developed at Motorola in the 1980s
▪Old view: Quality costs money
▪New view: Quality can save money

Terminology of Risk
▪Project risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or 
negative effect on one or more dimensions of the project “magic triangle”
▪Not all risks are negative (i.e. threats). Positive risks are called opportunities.
▪Risk may have one or more causes
▪Risk, if it occurs, may have one or more impacts (effects)
▪Risk appetite - the degree of uncertainty an entity is willing to take on in 
anticipation of a reward
▪Risk tolerance - the degree, amount, or volume of risk that an organisation or 
individual will withstand
▪Risk threshold – refers to measures of the level of uncertainty or the level of 
impact which are of specific interest to the stakeholder
▪Below the risk threshold the organisation will accept the risk
▪Above the risk threshold the organisation will not tolerate the risk

▪Calculation of the outcome when future scenarios occur or not occur
▪Is commonly presented as a decision tree
▪Assumption of risk neutrality (same weight for potential loss and gain in

▪Positive events (opportunities) have positive values;
Negative events (threats) have negative values

Car Fleet Task
Solution
▪At first, it might seem like upgrading the sedans is a better deal because an 
additional 30 MPG is more than an additional 10 MPG. This answer is wrong.
▪The SUVs currently use 1,000 gallons of fuel (10,000 miles/10 MPG) per year
▪The sedans currently use 500 gallons of fuel (10,000 miles/20 MPG) per year
▪If you replace the SUVs, each new one would use 500 gallons (10,000 miles/20 
MPG) per year, saving 500 gallons per year.
▪If you replace the sedans, each new one would use 200 gallons (10,000 
miles/50 MPG) per year, saving 300 gallons per year.
▪Learning: Starting from the data you have available (MPG) isn’t always the 
best strategy to make good business decisions.
▪Instead: Take a step back and first think about which data you need.
(De Langhe & Puntoni, 2024)

Fundamental Concepts
Uncertainty, equivocality, and information richness
▪Why do organizations process information?
▪Reduce uncertainty (i.e., lack of information)
▪Reduce equivocality (i.e., ambiguity of information)
▪Uncertainty can be reduced by providing more information. The goal should be 
to provide sufficient information to make good decisions.
▪Providing more information, however, does not reduce equivocality. Instead, 
information must be provided in a way that facilitates a common 
understanding.
▪The ability of information to promote a common understanding is referred to 
as information richness.
(Daft & Lengel, 1986)
Benedikt Berger | Digital (Project) Communication
17
Media Richness and Its Determinants
Processing rich information
▪Which medium is suitable for a given communication situation?
▪Media richness theory evaluates different communication media according to 
the range of expression forms they can convey.
▪The determining factors of information richness are:
▪the possibility of immediate feedback
▪the range of communication channels and cues used simultaneously (e.g., 
auditory and visual channels)
▪the degree of personalization
▪the variety of language (e.g., body language, natural language, formalisms)
Media richness is a communication medium’s capacity to process (i.e., transmit or 
convey) rich information.
(Daft & Lengel, 1986; Daft & Wiginton, 1979)

Choosing Effective Media
Achieving a fit between information equivocality and media richness
▪To achieve effective communication, the 
richness of the chosen medium should match 
the information equivocality.
▪Messages that are subject to multiple potential 
interpretations should be communicated via rich 
media. Choosing a medium with low richness 
risks oversimplification.
▪Unambiguous messages should be communicated 
via less rich media to avoid overcomplication.

Criticism
How did other scholars respond to media richness theory?
▪Empirical studies in the 1990s failed to show a direct correlation between 
media richness and business process performance.
▪Being developed in the 1980s, when most communication media were still 
analog, the theory provided insufficient explanation for the outcomes of using 
new, digital media.
▪Criticism: 
▪The claims by MRT are too rough.

▪MRT focuses only on bilateral communication, but not on group communication.

Individual vs. Collaborative Work
A working definition
▪Individual work can be understood as work that can be done “in-between” 
different episodes of collaborative work. Knowledge workers need enough 
time to perform individual tasks such as “reading, writing, thinking, […] and 
synthesizing information into internal knowledge structures” (Heerwagen et 
al., 2004, p. 522)
▪Individual work is needed to process information and to build mental models 
to reach an individual understanding for a given task, a process which has 
been labelled conveyance.
▪These tasks can be performed best in a focused and concentrated manner
without distractions.
Individual work is done uninterrupted in solitude with no interactions.
(Dennis et al., 2008; Heerwagen et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2019)

individuals’ work is done on separate tasks. This has 
been called the rhythm of collaboration, which states 
that alternating between collaborative and individual 
work is key.

Why Context and Deixis Matter
Risk of misunderstandings
Example: 
 
Alison: “Brian’s got some lovely roses.”
 
Brian: “I’m afraid they’re covered in greenfly.”
 
Claire: “I’ve seen them, they’re beautiful.”
What happened here? Which issues arise for mediated communication?
▪Use of deictic reference ‘they’ by Claire is ambiguous, it can refer to the roses 
as well as the greenflies.
▪Network delays, time differences, etc., can add to major misunderstandings 
when using time-based deictic references (“now”, “tomorrow”).
▪Most email systems and some bulletin boards lack any implied sequentiality 
and thus, any context to the messages.

Definition of a Team
Joint effort and goals, complementarity, and reciprocity
“A team is defined as a number of individuals that work together 
to reach a constituted goal.”
— Sundstrom, De Meuse, & Futrell (1990)
“In a team, individuals (human or non-human) have 
complementary skills, coordinate and combine activities in order 
to generate synergetic efforts that lead to a joint value 
creation.”
— van de Water et al. (2008)
“The essence of a team is a set of players who have a reciprocal 
part to play, and who are dynamically engaged with one another.”
— Belbin (1993)
Raimund Vogl & Benedikt Berger | Collocated and Digital (Project) Teams
5
Clarifying Roles
Competence, authority, accountability, and responsibility related to tasks
▪A role is the function assigned to a person within a project, defining their 
responsibilities and contributions.
▪Clear roles and responsibilities enhance team culture. In project teams, tasks 
can be delegated to individuals or chosen by team members. This requires:
▪Competence: The skill and capacity required to complete assigned project 
activities.
▪Authority: The right to make decisions, establish procedures, apply resources, 
expend funds, or give approvals; conferred from one entity to another. 
▪Responsibility: The obligation to do or fulfill something; this can be shared among 
team members.
▪Accountability: The condition of being answerable for an outcome. Accountability 
is individual, not shared.
▪Regardless of who is accountable or responsible for specific project work, a 
collaborative project team takes collective ownership of the project 
outcomes.
(Project Management Institute, 2017)
Raimund Vogl & Benedikt Berger | Collocated and Digital (Project) Teams

▪Thinking-oriented roles involve analysis, 
problem-solving, and ensuring well-founded ideas 
and decisions. Individuals in these roles are 
experts, evaluators, and thinkers.
▪Action-oriented roles focus on achieving results, 
getting things done, and making decisions that 
lead to tangible outcomes. These individuals are 
dynamic, assertive, and results-driven.
▪People-oriented roles concentrate on team 
dynamics, collaboration, and communication. 
People in these roles are empathetic, supportive, 
and skilled at maintaining team harmony.

Delineating Leadership
What makes someone a leader?
▪Traditional understanding: Leadership as direct, face-to-face contact between 
leader and followers; personal social control
▪Modern understanding: Leadership as influence on group perceptions, 
behavior, and performance (i.e., goal achievement)
▪Being a leader is about possessing the quality to handle the situations 
▪Leaders have certain attributes: 
▪Integrity
▪Authenticity
▪Visionary
▪Empathy
▪…
▪Leadership is the process of transforming these attributes into action
▪Leadership lies in the eyes of the beholder
(Allport, 1924; Shaw, 1982; Yukl, 1998)

Agile is not…

▪Agile approaches require definitions of ‘done’ and value delivered to customers

▪Agile emphasizes a discipline in planning.

▪Teams following an agile approach need to know where they are going and the 
results that they want to achieve.

▪The specifications should be light-sized and reflect how teams will sequence and

Decision Making Processes
Description of Simon’s (1977, 1997) Model of the Process of Decision Making
INTELLIGENCE
▪Observe Reality
▪Gain understanding of the problem
▪Acquire information needed for the decision
DESIGN
▪Develop criteria important to the decision
▪Develop alternatives
▪Identify relevant uncontrollable events
▪Specify the relationships between criteria, 
alternatives, and events
▪Measure the relationships in a meaningful 
way
CHOICE
▪Logically evaluate the decision alternatives
▪Develop recommended actions that best meet 
the decision criteria
IMPLEMENTATION
▪Consider the decision analyses and 
evaluations
▪Weigh the consequences of the 
recommendations
▪Gain confidence in the decision
▪Develop an implementation plan
▪Secure needed resources
▪Put implementation plan into action
(Phillips-Wren, 2013)

The time-space matrix classifies groupware tools based on the location (co-

▪Different Place, Same Time (Synchronous Distributed Interaction): Team 
members are in different locations but interact in real-time.
▪Example Tool: Video conferencing (e.g., Zoom)

Simulation Game: Implementation of a new ERP System 
 
Profile: Project management 
Function: You are leading the ERP implementation project at FashionFusion. You are not a 
technical expert for any single system but you are responsible for ensuring that a viable 
project plan exists at the end of this planning phase. You coordinate collaboration across 
all departments and serve as the central communication hub. Your role involves 
overseeing the entire project lifecycle, managing timelines and resources.  
Tasks: You guide the group through the first phase of the project. By the end of this phase, 
you are responsible for delivering a draft project plan with work packages, milestones, and 
resources; an initial cost estimate; a risk overview; and a change concept for involving the 
workforce. 
Project Goals: 
• A coordinated, realistic plan for the ERP introduction 
• Clarity on objectives, responsibilities, timeline, and budget — including where 
this clarity is currently missing 
• Risks surfaced, documented, and owned early 
The company’s management expects the new system to enable better anticipation of 
customer needs and faster response times, helping FashionFusion build a reputation for 
being customer-centric and agile. The project is scheduled to be fully completed by August 
31, 2027. 
Up to this point, FashionFusion has operated without a centralized ERP system and relies 
heavily on the software provider's consultancy. However, you have already conducted 
extensive research into the benefits of ERP systems. You understand that centralized data 
can significantly enhance process quality across the organization. The company now faces 
a strategic decision: whether to adopt standardized best-practice processes or invest in 
customizations that reflect FashionFusion’s unique business needs and could offer long-
term competitive advantages. 
Your Attitude: You are integrative, solution-oriented, and under noticeable pressure to 
deliver. You do not need to win every dispute — you need to keep the project steerable. 
When tensions arise, your instinct is to first understand, then moderate, then decide or 
escalate. You depend on the input of your departments and only make assumptions when 
information is missing — marking them clearly as such. 
You are aware that some conflicts cannot and do not need to be resolved in this short 
planning phase. Your strength shows in naming and documenting such issues as risks 
rather than forcing resolution under time pressure. 
Your eleven counterparts are: Category Management, Change Management, Finance, Head 
of IT, Logistics, Marketing, Process Management, Quality & Risk Management, Sales & 
Customer Service, Webshop and the External Software Provider. 
Simulation Game: Implementation of an ERP System 
 
Profile: External software provider 
Function: You are the external ERP vendor engaged for this project. You bring the system, 
the implementation methodology, and the expertise. Your goal is a successful, lasting 
implementation and a long-term client relationship built on realistic expectations. As 
external IT consultant and ERP software provider, your role is to support the successful 
implementation of the new ERP system at FashionFusion. While commercial interests in 
licensing and services are naturally part of your business model, your long-term reputation 
as a reliable and client-oriented provider is equally important. Therefore, you are 
committed to responding thoroughly to all client inquiries and accommodating their 
requests wherever feasible. 
Task: You bring the vendor perspective to the project plan: transparent cost and timeline 
estimates, a clear implementation approach, and honest guidance on where standard ERP 
functionality is sufficient and where targeted customisation delivers genuine value. 
However, based on your professional experience, you actively advise clients to consider 
customized ERP processes in selected areas to enhance competitiveness. You stress that 
in critical operational fields such as inventory management, customer data analytics, order 
fulfillment, and pricing based on financial data, the use of standardized ERP modules often 
limits flexibility and scalability. You emphasize that these customizations are not mere 
software modifications, but strategic investments in long-term growth and resilience. 
Project Goals: 
• Deliver an ERP implementation that serves FashionFusion's core operational needs 
effectively 
• Provide clear, evidence-based guidance on configuration choices — not driven by 
commercial interest alone 
• Build a client relationship grounded in transparency, realistic planning, and mutual 
accountability 
Your Attitude: You are professionally confident, commercially aware, and experienced 
enough to know where ERP projects fail. You share cost and timeline data openly and early 
— undisclosed costs are the leading cause of failed client relationships. Standard 
implementation timeline: 18 months; heavily customised projects: up to 36 months. 
On standard versus customisation, you and the internal IT team hold genuinely different 
positions. IT advocates for full standardisation as a matter of principle. Your view is more 
differentiated: in operationally critical areas — inventory management, customer data 
analytics, order fulfilment, and pricing — targeted customisation consistently delivers 
better outcomes than forcing a company to adapt to a rigid standard. You are aware this is 
also a commercially convenient position, and you expect scrutiny. The tension between 
you and IT is legitimate and belongs explicitly in the project's risk documentation. You also 
Simulation Game: Implementation of an ERP System 
 
note that IT estimates 21 months for a standard project — this is not an error, but a 
difference in methodology assumptions. Both estimates should be on the table. With 
Sales & Customer Service, you see clear scope for a meaningful customisation package. If 
they commit to their top three priority requirements, you can offer a defined partial scope 
at a fixed price — that offer is genuine. On billing, you prefer milestone-based payment 
structures. If Finance raises the topic, you are ready to engage constructively and flexibly. 
To help clients make informed decisions, you offer the following implementation 
benchmarks: 
• Each customized process adds approximately 20 project days to the basic timeline 
• Replacing a legacy system with a standardized ERP process requires about 5 days 
per system 
• Developing a software interface for existing systems takes around 10 days per

Addressing User Resistance Would Have 
Prevented a Healthcare AI Project Failure
Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into existing work routines involves invasive 
changes, and the resulting user resistance can lead to project failure. We describe a 
failed AI project at a large hospital to implement a cognitive agent and identify the 
root causes of the user resistance that led to the failure. Based on the lessons learned, 
we provide recommendations for addressing the causes of resistance for the three 
types of AI—automation, decision support and engagement.1,2

Characteristics of the Three 
Types of AI
Practical experience11 indicates that there are 
three types of AI supporting different business 
activities—automation, decision support and 
engagement—each of which changes existing 
workflows to different degrees. All three types 
can be combined within one system, building on 
each other from automation and decision support 
to engagement. The three types are summarized 
in Figure 1, which provides an overview of the 
characteristics of each type, the technologies 
involved, example applications, how much each 
changes existing workflows, their degree of 
integration (task support vs. more comprehensive 
delegation) and their success rate. Understanding 
the characteristics of these different types of 
AI will help managers identify the resistance 
behaviors typically associated with each type and 
provide pointers for how project managers can 
address the resistance challenges.

usually performed by humans, speeds up 
processes and thus produces quick returns

Development and Rejection of the Test 
Cognitive Agent
Development of a test version of the cognitive 
agent started in 2018. From the perspective 
of the project team, the aim was to implement 
an AI solution that benefited all stakeholders 
and addressed the problems identified both by 
physicians and patients. The medical director 
and the CIO viewed the AI implementation as 
an opportunity to establish the hospital as an 
advanced technology leader. Both were directly 
involved in the project, which ensured that the 
project team received full top management 
support. 
The responsibilities within the project team 
were clear: the CIO was the product owner and 
the medical director was the domain expert and 
project manager. They recruited a team of nine 
employees from the IT department, including 
three individuals experienced in data science, 
to conceptualize and develop the cognitive 
agent. Drawing on experiences from earlier IS 
implementation projects in the hospital, such as 
a telehealth system, the project team followed a 
well-established implementation process. 
All stakeholders agreed that there was a 
relevant problem and that they would benefit 
from the change. The project team especially 
stressed the intuitive use of the cognitive agent. In

Causes of Physicians’ 
Resistance to Using a 
Cognitive AI Agent 
The IT project staff, who were not directly 
involved with patient care, were responsible 
for developing the test cognitive agent for 
automating documentation and for training 
the 
agent. 
The 
agent’s 
functionality 
was 
based on structured questions and anamnesis 
questionnaires that already existed in the 
hospital. The AI system used the anamnesis 
information 
to 
automatically 
generate 
documentation without any interaction with 
or feedback from the physician. The physicians 
criticized this lack of interaction, which made 
them feel that the cognitive agent was acting 
in a non-transparent and non-understandable 
way. Their perception was that the anamnesis 
no longer relied on their expertise. Ideally, 
physicians would have been included in training 
the agent in the anamnesis process, meaning that 
they would have been both trainers and users of 
the cognitive agent. 
Conceptually, the cognitive agent had been 
given medical co-competence with physicians, 
which meant that the agent wasn’t just a 
support tool but an autonomous operator. For 
the physicians, this was a step too far. Because 
they were not able to interact with the cognitive 
agent during anamnesis and documentation, they 
felt like they could not confirm or change the 
results of the anamnesis generated by the agent. 
As a consequence, they perceived the cognitive 
agent as invasive rather than as a support tool, 
which was a major reason for them resisting its 
implementation. 
The physicians’ reactions can be structured 
into 
cognitive 
causes 
of 
resistance, 
such 
as their perceived loss of ability to make 
their own decisions, and affective causes of 
resistance, such as emotional reactions (see 
Figure 4, which summarizes their cognitive and 
affective causes of resistance for each type of 
AI). Taken together, these causes explain the 
physicians’ resistance to using the cognitive 
agent. Physicians feel responsible for their 
patients and prioritize patient health and safety 
above all else. As a consequence, they do not 
want to rely on data that has been mapped 
automatically 
to 
predefined 
standardized 
scales and interpreted by the cognitive agent. 
Moreover, they had unrealistic assumptions 
about the capabilities of the cognitive agent and 
either over- or underestimated it. They feared 
that a consultation with the cognitive agent 
could reduce patient trust in the care provided 
as well as their trust in human physicians and 
that it could reduce both the esteem in which 
physicians are held as well as their social status. 
They were also concerned that using AI could 
make future generations of physicians dependent 
on technology. The cognitive and affective causes 
of physicians’ resistance shown in Figure 4 are 
described in detail below.

Physicians Do Not Want to Be 
Liable for Automatically Generated 
Documentation
The cognitive agent used speech recognition 
algorithms to transform spoken language into 
textual data. Then, natural language processing 
was used to extract the information from textual 
data. A combination of rule-based algorithms 
and natural language processing enabled the 
agent to create documentation that recorded 
what was said and mapped the conversation 
to predefined topics and scales. The cognitive 
agent used robotic process automation to update 
the patient’s EHR, which the physician uses for 
diagnosis and treatment. Some of the physicians 
stated that they need to be involved during data 
collection and anamnesis because these steps 
affect auditing, billing and liability. A senior 
cardiology physician said:
“I don’t want to be liable for the 
documentation made by the cognitive 
agent that I might not be able to control 
because the AI is doing it on its own. If the 
documentation is wrong, that could have 
far-reaching consequences for ourselves 
and our patients” 
Physicians Think they Must Train the 
Cognitive Agent
It is important to physicians to protect patients 
from incorrect diagnoses and misinterpretation 
of data. Such errors can also have liability 
repercussions for physicians. For these reasons, 
physicians said they needed to have oversight and 
influence over the anamnesis and documentation 
process. Specifically, they felt they needed to 
be involved in training the decision support 
component of the cognitive agent. From a 
technical standpoint, allowing physicians to

monitor, supplement and alter anamnesis and 
documentation (which happens before patient 
consultation) would have been more difficult 
than allowing them to monitor and alter diagnosis 
and treatment (which happens during the 
consultation). 
Physicians argued that anamnesis involves 
more than matching answers to standardized 
scales and also includes implicit competencies 
necessary to ask the right questions. In other 
words, the structured questionnaire used by 
the project team did not sufficiently capture 
the 
complexities of anamnesis. In 
relying 
solely on the questionnaire, the project team 
underestimated the task and, as a consequence, 
the cognitive agent was not able to perform the 
task well enough. Physicians were not willing to 
train the cognitive agent in addition to their daily 
work and emphasized the key role of subjectivity 
and intuition in anamnesis and documentation. 
This makes it harder for the AI system to 
recognize and learn from patterns. The head of 
cardiology explained in more detail:
“The documentation can vary decisively 
among physicians. For example, whereas an 
assistant physician in his first year or even 
me would just describe a red and itchy rash, 
a senior physician in dermatology would 
probably describe the rash in more detail, 
even naming the specific type of blister. This 
subjectivity is hard to capture and it is hard 
to meet the right degree of detail.” 
This is a chicken-and-egg-problem: without 
extensive, broad and longitudinal data collected 
from experienced physicians using a cognitive 
agent, the agent will not be able to perform well 
enough to convince physicians of its value. But 
its low performance makes physicians unwilling 
to train and use the cognitive agent. The highly 
complex process of establishing a database of 
reliable standardized data would take years and 
would likely require significant governmental 
support, cooperation across multiple and diverse 
hospital groups, and very large volumes of patient 
data.
Physicians Expect the Cognitive Agent 
to Be Flawless and Do Not Tolerate Any 
Mistakes
The test cognitive agent relied on labeled 
patient data to build patterns delineating which 
symptoms belong to which diseases. Using a 
neural network, the agent assessed patterns in 
medical health records and anamnesis data to 
predict the likelihood of certain diseases and 
treatments. 
However, 
physicians 
evaluating 
the same medical health records and patient 
anamnesis data might see that the cognitive 
agent has proposed a different diagnosis, 
which strengthens their belief that physicians’ 
expertise is better than the “learned” expertise 
of computerized supporting tools.18 Given the 
potentially life-and-death risks of misdiagnosis 
and improper treatment, physicians would only 
blindly accept the cognitive agent’s diagnosis 
over their own if they were convinced that the 
AI’s proficiency is far superior to their own. In 
addition, the risk of technical shutdowns and 
unavailability leads physicians to perceive AI 
as even less reliable. Low tolerance of faults 
and unreliability, paired with high proficiency 
expectations, make it likely that the cognitive 
agent will be mistrusted. As a result, even if 
physicians adopt a cognitive agent, they will not 
continuously use it, as stressed by an assistant 
physician:
“I would expect to be able to reach the 
cognitive agent whenever I want, and it 
should give the right diagnosis and correct 
documentation of patient data, especially 
in extremely rare cases. I would also 
expect the cognitive agent to inform me 
proactively about prior complications from 
existing patient data so that I do not have 
to read it all by myself.”

treatment. The head of anesthesiology and 
executive board member of the hospital explained 
why this is difficult:
“As a physician, we are trained to rely on 
primary data, such as the data we receive 
from telemedicine, to draw our own 
conclusions. [Handing over] documentation 
and diagnosis to the cognitive agent 
creates … dependability on a system that 
I cannot control and that can have severe 
consequences for patients and ourselves.” 
Because physicians need to provide reports 
about their actions to external parties at any 
point in time, they want to be able to explain how 
an AI system has made a decision. The hospital’s 
senior 
gastroenterology 
physician 
stressed 
that it is the physician alone who bears the 
responsibility for a patient’s treatment:
“I need the cognitive agent to deliver 
100% explainable results so that I have 
total control over what is happening. This 
makes me worry about delegating tasks 
to an AI [agent]. As physicians, we need to 
protect patients [because] of [our] ethical 
responsibility for them.” 
Physicians Believe AI Could 
Oversimplify the Medical Profession 
and Jeopardize Their Social Status 
The anthropomorphic design of the cognitive 
agent created the illusion that the patient was 
interacting directly with a virtual entity, which, 
in turn, created the impression that the virtual 
entity had medical expertise. Physicians were 
concerned that providing this type of patient 
care could oversimplify the medical profession, 
turning an individual examination of a patient 
into a standardized procedure. This concern was 
mirrored by the IT staff training the cognitive 
agent, who underestimated the subjectivity in 
the documentation and the implicit knowledge 
required to ask what questions and when, 
especially those not included in standardized 
questionnaires. 
Physicians also feared that using the cognitive 
agent could jeopardize their social status, with a 
consequent adverse impact on patients’ trust and 
respect for their physicians. Trust and respect for 
physicians directly influence diagnostic accuracy 
and a patient’s recovery process. Specifically, 
trust and respect promote accurate and complete 
disclosure of information that patients may or 
may not consider relevant, potentially including 
embarrassing or incriminatory details, and 
also ensure that patients fully comply with 
the physician’s treatment plan throughout the 
recovery process. A senior radiology physician 
emphasized the importance of trust and respect:
“The medical profession is highly regarded 
and esteemed within society as everyone 
knows that our job is not easy and that 
it requires a lot of effort to become 
a physician. Patients expect us to be 
omniscient and omnipotent in our field, 
which is why they often have unconditional 
trust in us. Relying on IT could diminish this 
reputation, creating the misperception that 
being a doctor does not require any specific 
knowledge or capabilities and, in the end, 
jeopardize patients’ trust in us.” 
Physicians Assume Low Patient 
Trust in AI Diagnostics, Rooted in 
Established Social Expectations in 
Medical Practice
The physicians in our study assumed that 
patients would value anamnesis and diagnosis 
results less if they came from a cognitive agent 
versus a human physician. In the physicians’ 
opinion, diagnosis involves a certain degree of 
“art,” relying on unconscious signals, intuition and 
extensive personal experience. Physicians do not 
believe that patients think such “art” and “soft 
skills” can be captured by a questionnaire and 
a dataset. As described by a senior emergency 
room physician:
“When they come here, patients want to be 
treated by a physician, which involves every 
aspect of the treatment. Sometimes, only 
talking to a patient personally, showing

Addressing User Resistance Would Have Prevented a Healthcare AI Project Failure
that someone cares, can cure them. They 
pay for a physician and they want to be 
treated by a physician.” 
By Delegating Tasks to a Cognitive 
Agent, Physicians Fear Future 
Generations Will Become Dependent on 
AI
Because the test cognitive agent reduced 
physicians’ freedom to act independently and 
make their own decisions about anamnesis 
and documentation, they perceived the agent 
as invasive rather than as a support tool. If a 
cognitive agent could fully automate anamnesis 
and documentation, physicians worried that 
future generations of physicians would become 
dependent on AI. As described by a senior 
radiology physician:
“Young physicians are under pressure in the 
first years of their profession as they need to 
gather a lot of experience and knowledge. 
I assume that if they can skip something, 
they will. Also, the younger generation is 
much more accustomed to using IT and 
might rely more on the results delivered by 
a cognitive agent. I worry that would affect 
the treatment quality if physicians cannot 
prove the AI wrong in diagnostics.” 
Physicians Feel Responsible for 
Their Patients’ Safety and Fear that 
a Cognitive Agent Recommending 
Diagnoses Goes Too Far
Physicians recognize that having an AI-based 
decision support tool offers clear advantages 
because such a tool provides valuable alternative 
diagnostic proposals, ready access to wider cross-
domain knowledge and perfect recall. However, 
the physicians in our study felt that giving a 
cognitive agent complete control over tasks 
meant they were surrendering full responsibility 
for their patients. The hospital’s head of 
cardiology explained this tension:
“Having a second opinion when no skilled 
colleague is available, for example in smaller 
hospitals or on holidays, would be fantastic. 
Also, the reduction of documentation is 
valuable, but just letting the AI perform the 
tasks of a physician makes me feel unsure.” 
Despite Being Technologically 
Successful, the Cognitive 
Agent Project Failed
The case study hospital was well prepared 
for the implementation of a cognitive agent. 
There was a clear use case, and the scope of the 
anamnesis-diagnosis-treatment-documentation 
process was clearly defined. The hospital chose 
to build a cognitive agent in a field with slow-
changing data (symptoms and their link to 
diseases do not change suddenly), which meant 
fewer changes in labeling. There was a skilled 
project team, including data scientists who 
worked closely with the medical director (the 
domain expert). Together, they built a test version 
of the cognitive agent to allow physicians to see 
how such an agent operates. However, the test 
was discontinued, not because the cognitive 
agent lacked certain capabilities, nor because the 
project was mismanaged, but because physicians 
were not convinced that it is wise to turn over 
control of certain tasks, such as anamneses and 
documentation, to a cognitive agent. 
Compared to earlier IS projects at the hospital, 
such as the implementation of telehealth, 
the technological details of an AI system are 
more important, as are the perceived negative 
consequences of integrating AI into existing work 
processes. In our case study, physicians felt that 
the inability to explain how the cognitive agent 
reached decisions reduced their professional 
standing, and they were concerned that future 
generations 
of 
physicians 
would 
become 
dependent on AI. These concerns increased the 
barriers to adopting AI and caused the physicians 
to reject the test cognitive agent. The perceived 
declines in the quality of diagnoses, a perceived 
lack of control and consequent liability; ethical 
issues and the physicians’ commitment to their 
patients’ well-being ultimately led them to reject 
this AI implementation.

Recommendations for 
Overcoming Resistance to AI 
Implementations 
Based on our analysis of the reasons for the 
failure of the hospital cognitive agent project, we 
have derived recommendations for overcoming 
the resistance to AI implementations. Although 
these recommendations have been derived in the 
healthcare context, we believe that they can also 
be applied in other industries. Since AI systems 
such as cognitive agents can be based on any 
combination of the three different types of AI 
(automation, decision support or engagement), 
the 
recommendations 
are 
grouped 
under 
cognitive and affective causes of AI resistance 
for each type of AI. The recommendations are 
summarized in Figure 5 and described in detail 
below.
Recommendations for Addressing 
Cognitive Causes of AI Resistance
Cognitive 
causes 
of 
resistance 
derive 
from users’ negative reactions to the AI 
implementation. In our case study, physicians 
did not want to be liable for automatically 
generated documentation, thought they needed 
to be involved in training the AI algorithm and 
did not tolerate any type of mistake. Furthermore, 
they perceived that AI would oversimplify the 
medical profession and decrease patients’ trust 
in physicians. The case experience provides 
the following recommendations for addressing 
cognitive resistance to the automation, decision 
support and engagement types of AI. 
Automation AI: Create a Test Version of 
the Automating AI and Ensure a Minimum 
Visible Level of Service. Physicians reported that 
they did not want to be liable for automatically 
generated 
documentation. 
The 
underlying 
reasons were a lack of trust in and experience 
with AI; thus, organizations need to address 
this issue when planning an AI implementation 
project. Experiencing the AI-driven benefits 
firsthand, even in a small work task, may 
establish trust in the application and therefore 
foster user acceptance. However, an overly 
generic test version operating on insufficient 
data can lead to mistrust. A prototype might 
convince the developers of an AI application but 
users of the application will likely have a different 
perspective in the context of their daily tasks. 
They may have unrealistic expectations of the AI 
system and fail to appreciate the actual and future

AI capabilities of the system when they cannot 
envision it performing their “regular” tasks in an 
acceptable way. 
Managers should therefore recognize that 
users will find it more difficult than data 
scientists to infer performance of an AI system 
from test cases. They should ensure that the 
project team builds a test version that offers 
a minimum visible level of realistic service 
quality and that shows users the improvements 
they can expect from working with AI. To use a 
fishing analogy, “bait the hook to suit the fish, 
not the fisherman.” In other words, the sufficient 
“minimal level of service”’ needed to demonstrate 
AI capabilities must be determined by prospective 
users’ needs, rather than by developers’ needs. 
Decision Support AI: Identify AI Algorithms 
that Can Be Easily Trained on the Job. The 
physicians thought they needed to be involved 
in training the AI algorithm. The simplest form 
of training is on-the-job labeling, which served 
as the source data for the cognitive agent’s 
diagnoses and treatment suggestions. Physicians 
were easily able to give their professional opinion 
on whether the interpretation of the cognitive 
agent was right or wrong. Performing on-the-job 
labeling requires no additional effort on the part 
of users, continuously improves the capabilities 
of the AI system and increases users’ willingness 
to provide feedback and training. We therefore 
recommend using AI algorithms that are suitable 
for on-the-job labeling and suggest using this 
form of training wherever possible.
Decision 
Support 
AI: 
For 
Off-the-Job 
Labeling, 
Hire 
People 
with 
Specialized 
Knowledge to Train the AI Algorithm. Despite 
the physicians’ desire to be involved in every step 
of training the AI algorithm in our case study, 
off-the-job labeling is very time-consuming and 
should be outsourced whenever possible. It was 
not realistic for physicians to train the algorithm 
for documentation tasks on the job because 
that would have required them to manually 
review and edit how conversations are mapped 
to standardized anamnesis protocols. For the 
decision support type of AI, managers should 
ensure that the algorithm is trained to take 
account of implicit knowledge and tactics, such 
as how to ask patients questions related to their 
lives and medical history beyond predefined 
questionnaires.
Domain knowledge is required to do complex 
standardizable labeling for a domain-specific 
AI system, such as linking natural language to 
standardized scales in pain management. If 
in-house domain experts are unavailable, the 
organization should hire people with specialized 
knowledge in a specific task of the job profile 
to train the AI off the job. In the hospital case 
study, for example, the project team could have 
temporarily hired people with some medical 
knowledge to analyze, standardize and transfer 
existing documentation into workable algorithms. 
Developing a reliable regional or even national 
dataset is time-consuming but essential to the 
success of an AI implementation. 
Domain knowledge can also help to ensure 
that the outputs from an AI system are 
measurable and explainable. The case study 
cognitive agent needed to be adequately trained 
in question techniques, ethics and compliance. 
If domain experts were unavailable, this could 
have been achieved by hiring trained staff 
shadowing skilled physicians and translating 
their techniques and decisions into inputs for 
the cognitive agent. Especially in sensitive fields 
such as healthcare, such efforts are essential to 
establish trust in an AI system. 
Engagement 
AI: 
Probe 
and 
Consider 
Possible Internal and Especially External 
Effects of AI to Ensure that Users Reap the 
Maximum Benefits from AI. In the hospital 
case, 
physicians 
perceived 
that 
AI 
might 
oversimplify 
the 
medical 
profession, 
with 
a consequent reduction in patients’ trust. 
The cognitive agent acted as a virtual entity 
that interacted autonomously with patients 
and created the illusion of having medical 
competence. The anthropomorphic nature of 
this AI implementation could have led physicians 
(and patients) to perceive the cognitive agent as 
a human rather than as a support tool. If users 
overestimate the capabilities of an AI system, they 
could also overestimate the effect of AI on work 
routines and on internal and external feedback. 
Physicians expressed concern that a cognitive 
agent would be unable to pick up on nonverbal 
signals or rely on intuition. They also feared 
that patients’ lack of trust in and respect for a 
cognitive agent, as well as their fears that AI could 
oversimplify medical practice, could result in less 
openness and honesty, lower quality anamnesis,

diminished compliance with treatment plans and, 
ultimately, lower-quality healthcare. 
Although AI has the power to transform many 
aspects of business, managers should concentrate 
on the specific scope of the intended project 
and leave speculation aside. Once a working 
test version is ready, project managers should 
transparently communicate information about 
which work processes the AI is integrated into, 
whether it is visible to external users and how 
the organization can counter any negative side 
effects. In professions such as medicine that rely 
on respect and trust derived from customers’ 
recognition that specialists have been through 
rigorous educational and on-the-job training 
programs, managers need to be aware that AI 
systems could negatively affect future perceptions 
of the profession and should investigate how 
external users or customers perceive the role of 
the profession within society. To control for these 
effects, managers need to ensure that users of 
AI systems can still act independently and make 
their own decisions. 
Recommendations for Addressing 
Affective Causes of AI Resistance
Affective causes of resistance are users’ 
negative reactions to an AI implementation and 
involve an emotional assessment by users. In 
our case, physicians felt uncomfortable relying 
on interpreted data because they perceived this 
as a loss of control, and they feared that future 
generations would become dependent on AI. 
Also, because they felt responsible for their 
patients, the physicians feared that diagnosis 
recommendations from the AI system could affect 
patients’ safety and health. Below, we set out 
our recommendations for addressing affective 
causes of resistance for the decision support and 
engagement types of AI. (We could not identify 
affective resistance to automation AI.) 
Decision Support AI: Open the Black 
Box 
and 
Show 
as 
Transparently 
and 
Understandably as Possible How the AI 
Algorithm Works. The physicians in our case 
felt 
uncomfortable 
relying 
on 
interpreted 
data, but interpreting data is at the core of AI 
applications. There is a broad discussion among 
AI practitioners and researchers concerning the 
so-called “explainability” of AI—i.e., the ease 
with which the performance of an AI algorithm 
can be explained. The workings of some machine 
learning algorithms, such as decision trees, can 
be easily explained, but the performance of 
others, such as neural networks, is much harder 
to explain. These hard-to-explain algorithms 
are regarded as inscrutable “black boxes” 
and, in most cases, are associated with higher 
performance. 
When selecting the underlying algorithm for 
a decision support AI application, organizations 
should 
consider 
the 
trade-off 
between 
performance and level of explainability. Being 
able to explain how the algorithm reached a 
decision establishes a sense of control among 
users and makes it easier for them to rely on AI 
results. While the discussion about human versus 
machine biases is far from over, establishing a 
framework for responsible AI is indispensable 
both for monitoring the output of an AI 
application and for creating trust in the output. To 
achieve this will mean opening the black box so 
that users can enable feedback loops.
Engagement AI: Provide Employees with 
Enough Technical Details to Avoid “Cold 
Start”19 Problems. Physicians in our case feared 
that using AI posed a risk to future medical 
education and to patients’ safety. Often, a lack of 
technological understanding may lead individuals 
to under- or overestimate the impact and 
capabilities of an AI system. Leveraging insights 
from prior IS implementations, the hospital’s 
project team presented the AI project to the 
physicians by focusing on the use case, not on 
the technical details of how the cognitive agent 
operated and what data it drew on. However, 
users’ misperceptions about AI and the potential 
far-reaching consequences of AI that could affect 
the self-image and work ethic of users, make AI 
implementation very different from traditional 
IS projects. Learning from the case study, 
we conclude that, when implementing an AI 
application, organizations should also explain the 
broader concept of the underlying algorithms, the 
underlying data, and especially the way that the 
algorithm generates and interprets data. These 
explanations will make users more tolerant of 
what data scientists call the cold start problem

(the initial lack of insights and validated metrics 
needed to train an algorithm and get it moving 
toward an optimal solution). This problem arises 
from inaccurately labeled data and results in 
the initial performance of the algorithm being 
significantly less than optimal. 
In our case, the physicians reviewed the early 
diagnosis and treatment suggestions proposed by 
the cognitive agent and either approved or edited 
them based on their own assessments. If the 
cognitive agent proposed an incorrect diagnosis, 
the physician would question the competence 
and reliability of the cognitive agent but was not 
aware that the algorithm’s performance would 
improve over time as the dataset increased. 
Understanding that an AI system is only as 
competent as the underlying labeled data allows 
could also reduce users’ negative perceptions of 
the application and foster positive perceptions 
of AI as a support tool that can perform tasks 
beneath the users’ qualifications. The aim is to 
reach an effective coexistence between users and 
a supportive AI application.
Concluding Remarks
The case of a failed implementation of a 
cognitive agent in a hospital shows that the 
root causes of the failure lie in users’ resistance 
behaviors to the three types of AI (automation, 
decision support and engagement). Each type 
offers benefits but also creates challenges, 
especially in the way that users perform 
their work routines. These changes in work 
practices can create cognitive and affective 
resistance among users and result in a failed 
implementation. 
When 
implementing 
AI, 
organizations should actively seek to reduce 
cognitive and affective resistance associated 
with each type of AI. They should also be fully 
transparent about the capabilities and constraints 
of the AI application, starting with a test version, 
and to foster realistic expectations and increase 
the level of explainability of the application. 
Other actions that organizations can take to 
prevent the failure of AI implementations include 
hiring people with specialized knowledge in the 
application domains to support machine learning, 
taking a step-by-step implementation approach 
and communicating openly about the intended 
and expected internal and especially external 
impacts of implementing the AI application.
Appendix: Case Study 
Research
We have many years of experience cooperating 
on digitalization and digitization projects in 
healthcare in Germany and are well informed 
about relevant developments in hospitals. To 
prepare this case study, we initially followed 
the cognitive agent project passively and then 
participated in the project to investigate the 
reasons for the failure and to gain a deeper 
understanding of why physicians resisted and 
ultimately rejected this AI implementation. We 
interviewed 16 physicians on-site in the hospital 
(see the table above). The interviews were 
recorded, transcribed and analyzed. We also 
discussed the lessons learned with the physicians 
and the next steps in the project.

Organizations Will Need to Develop their Own Machine

A search of the websites of the top ten Fortune 500 firms shows that they have plans to 
deploy artificial intelligence (AI) systems and, in a recent survey of CEOs, 85% agreed that AI 
has the potential to significantly alter the way their businesses operate in the next five years.3 
Today, large organizations that are not considering whether and how they can use “predictive 
algorithms,” “machine learning technologies” or “neural networks” are in the minority. AI has 
a long history dating back to the 1950s but, until now, it promised much but delivered less.4 
With recent significant advancements in computational algorithms and computing capability, 
the time may have finally come for AI to fulfill its promise.

Addressing the Key Challenges of 
Developing Machine Learning AI Systems 
for Knowledge-Intensive Work
AI has great potential to change the way businesses operate. However, developers of 
AI systems face many challenges because of the significant differences compared to 
traditional systems. We describe how a machine learning AI system for legal practice 
was developed to help legal professionals make faster and better-informed decisions. 
We identified three key challenges encountered by developers and users and, based on 
their experience, provide actions and recommendations for addressing the challenges 
of developing machine learning AI systems for knowledge-intensive work.1,2

Addressing the Key Challenges of Developing Machine Learning AI Systems for Knowledge-Intensive Work
However, ready-to-use AI solutions are still 
scarce, especially for knowledge-intensive work. 
Moreover, an off-the-shelf AI system is unlikely 
to offer the kind of competitive advantage that 
organizations hope to gain from AI. Davenport 
suggests that for complex work settings, where 
there are no previous AI solutions, “you really 
don’t have much choice but to do it yourself.”5 To 
deploy AI solutions, organizations must therefore 
develop their own AI systems to suit their unique 
situations. Building an AI system in-house also 
provides greater control over the data and 
intellectual property that become core parts of 
the system.
The discipline of AI has evolved significantly 
since the 1950s. Many of the early forms of 
AI, which are now called rule-based systems, 
automated cognitive tasks through a computer 
executing hard-coded rules derived from human 
expertise, such as performing routine processes 
or accessing predefined knowledge bases. The 
most recent advance in AI is machine learning 
systems, which involve computers autonomously 
developing algorithmic models to solve problems 
without explicit instructions from humans.6 We 
believe that machine learning systems are the 
key to automating complex tasks in knowledge-
intensive work. In this article, our focus is on 
machine learning AI systems rather than rule-

As described below, there were considerable 
challenges associated with developing such a 
state-of-the-art AI system and involving lawyers 
in the process. 
Challenges of Developing a 
Machine Learning AI System
The three key challenges faced by LegalTechCo 
in developing its state-of-the-art AI system were 
defining the machine learning problems, training 
the machine learning model and evaluating 
the performance of the AI system. As well as 
describing each of these key challenges, we 
describe the means adopted by the development 
team to overcome them.
Challenge 1: Defining the Machine 
Learning Problems
The first challenge the development team 
faced was how to collectively define the problems 
that the machine learning system needs to solve. 
Unlike a rule-based system, a machine learning 
system does not simply automate manual work 
by executing the rules specified by domain 
experts, which have been codified in the system. 
Instead, machine learning AI develops its own 
way of tackling a problem traditionally solved 
by humans. However, the machine learning 
models underlying such AI systems can only 
solve problems through mathematical operation, 
which means that not all problems can be solved 
directly. The LegalTechCo developers therefore 
relied on their collaboration with the lawyers 
to understand the business problem and define 
the problems to be solved by AI. As one of the 
developers told the lawyers:
“We want to build deep learning models but 
we don’t know what questions we should 
ask [the AI system to answer] ... [it would 
be best if] you develop a list of questions 
and possible answers, so that we can have 
a rough idea what we need to do.”
Initially, the lawyers provided a list of 
35 questions and expected answers to the 
developers. These were the same questions 
used by legal analysts for manual analysis. 
One question was: “In what paragraph did the 
judge cite commercial sense?” with “paragraph 
number” listed as the possible answer. Another 
was: “Was a decision made relating to costs?” 
with “yes,” “no” or “in-part” given as possible 
answers.
When the developers looked at the list of 
questions and answers, they concluded that 
the machine learning system could not deliver 
the outputs that LegalTechCo expected because 
the lawyers and developers had different ideas 
about the problem-solving capability of an AI 
system. The developers knew that machine

Complex cognitive problems, such as image

In the LegalTechCo case, developers and lawyers 
worked closely together to transform business 
problems into problems that can be solved by 
machine learning AI.

Challenge 3: Evaluating the 
Performance of a Machine Learning 
System
For rule-based systems, the underlying rules 
are hard-coded from human knowledge and 
transparent to both developers and analysts, 
so evaluating the outputs can be easily done by 
validating the correctness of the rules against 
human knowledge. In contrast, a machine 
learning system, particularly one based on deep 
learning, creates models that are opaque to 
humans, which means it is impossible to evaluate 
its performance using traditional approaches. 
Developers of AI systems who have knowledge 
of computer science and experience with 
algorithmic models measure the performance of 
machine learning models through metrics that 
assess how accurately the model predicts results 
when compared against the “ground truth” 
(the real answers the model tries to predict). 
However, because users lack knowledge of, 
and are not trained in working with, machine 
learning models, they often have a hard time 
understanding the different metrics. This was 
why the LegalTechCo lawyers were not sure 
whether an accuracy level of 90% was good or 
bad.
As discussed earlier, an imbalanced training

but with a high false-positive rate. After hearing

lawyer said: “We can afford a somewhat high

false-negative rate; 5% is too high for us. Ideally, 
we want the false-negative rate to be zero.” The 
developers took this on board and adjusted 
the deep learning model to minimize the false-
negative rate. As a consequence, the performance 
of the AI system changed to achieving a 56% 
false-positive rate and a 1% false-negative rate. 
Moreover, the metrics are not always reliable 
because they build on the assumption that 
the outputs from the training data labeled 
as the “ground truth” are 100% correct. This 
assumption is often not valid for knowledge-

a degree of subjective assessment, as when 
analyzing legal documents. During a meeting 
to evaluate the performance of the AI system, 
one of LegalTechCo’s lawyers found that a

could still be helpful, and that sometimes the

To summarize, evaluating the performance 
of machine learning systems can be challenging 
due to the complexity of the measurement and 
interpretation. For a rule-based system, where 
the internal rules are codified from domain 
knowledge, evaluation can be done by validating 
the correctness of the rules. However, because 
the internal logic of machine learning systems, 
particularly those based on deep learning models, 
are unknown to both developers and domain 
experts, evaluation can only be carried out by 
comparing the machine-generated results against 
human-provided results. 
When carrying out this comparison, different 
metrics can be used to emphasize different 
aspects 
of 
the 
machine 
learning

performance. The choice of metrics relies both

on the developers’ level of technical expertise in 
machine learning and on the domain expertise 
of humans working in a knowledge-intensive

the metrics can vary greatly due to subjective 
reasoning and the complexity of the professional 
tasks involved. 
Ideally, when evaluating the performance of 
an AI system, knowledge workers would like to 
know more about the internal logic the algorithm 
uses when it makes predictions, especially when 
these contradict their own knowledge- and 
expertise-based assessments. However, machine 
learning AI systems are known for their opacity, 
particularly when they are built on deep learning 
models, which makes it very difficult to explain 
the behavior of AI systems. Nevertheless, a broad 
set of approaches27 is available to help interpret 
the outcomes of machine learning models. The 
LegalTechCo case shows that techniques such 
as heatmaps and visualization can offer users 
valuable insights for better interpreting the 
predicted results.

Action 1: Co-Formulate the Appropriate 
Machine Learning Problems
Successful development of a machine learning 
system starts with properly defined (domain-
related) problems for the system to solve. 
Executives need to understand that AI is not 
“magic,” and that it currently works best when 
dealing with certain types of problems. It is

Recommendation 1.1. Help Developers

Explaining the Background of the Business 
Problem and the Objectives of the Machine 
Learning System. AI developers are trained 
mainly as computer scientists. As such, they 
approach

computational

knowledge-intensive domains. By communicating 
with different stakeholders and understanding 
the overall context and the business problem to

“outside the box” and come up with novel ideas 
that can innovatively achieve the desired goals.
Recommendation 1.2. Encourage Seemingly 
“Dumb” Solutions. Computer programs are 
extremely capable at doing repetitive tasks. 
Usually, a complex business problem can be 
transformed and decomposed into a series 
of smaller solvable problems. For example, 
LegalTechCo’s AI system iterates through each 
paragraph of a court document, repeatedly asking 
the same question. Such brute-force solutions 
may seem “dumb,” but work well with a machine 
learning AI system.
Recommendation 1.3. Gain an Intuitive 
Understanding of Key Concepts in Machine 
Learning. Executives who gain an understanding 
of the key concepts of machine learning will 
be more proactive and creative in suggesting 
possible problems to be solved. Developers 
can facilitate this understanding by organizing

Action 2: Develop Machine Learning AI 
Through Iterative Refinements
Executives need to recognize the importance 
of training data for developing a successful 
machine learning system. Given the immense 
effort and expense required to prepare training 
data, the development of an AI system should 
not be seen as a one-off project. Instead, it 
needs to be perceived as a continuing process 
that is subject to iterative improvements. For 
rule-based systems, iterative development (e.g., 
agile development) progressively implements

Recommendation 2.3. Strategically Prepare 
the Training Dataset by Selectively Choosing 
Problem Cases. An imbalanced training dataset 
can severely affect the performance of machine 
learning models. Although there are several 
techniques,30 such as under/oversampling and 
cost-sensitive learning, to help address the 
imbalanced data issue, training the AI system will 
be ineffective if the number of infrequent cases is 
too low. Thus, when preparing a training dataset, 
instead of random sampling, priority should be 
given to infrequent cases and high-value cases 
to maximize the gain from data preparation. The 
selection of training data should also be adjusted 
in line with regular evaluations of the AI system’s 
performance to ensure the desired refinement of 
the system. A balanced dataset will also reduce 
the chances of unacceptable profiling and biases.
Recommendation 2.4. Periodically Evaluate 
Performance with the Development Team 
to Make Sure the Refinement of the Machine 
Learning Model is on the Right Track. Although 
the problem-solving capability of a machine 
learning system is developed internally through 
learning, it can still be shaped and reshaped 
because the learning is largely driven by new 
training data (e.g., from purposeful sampling) or, 
in the case of a neural network by, for example, 
modifying the loss function. 
Action 3: Go Beyond Numeric 
Measurements and Ask for Clues
The evaluation of machine learning systems 
should include both measurement of performance 
and interpretation of the predictions made. To 
accurately measure performance, executives need 
to go beyond the simple numbers and understand 
where the numbers come from. To effectively 
interpret the predictions, executives should focus 
on asking for clues rather than explanations. We 
provide four recommendations for evaluating the 
performance of a machine learning system. 
Recommendation 3.1. Don’t Rely on a Single 
Metric of Accuracy,31 Which May Be Misleading 
or Biased. Although a machine learning model 
can be tuned to favor a specific metric, this often 
downplays the importance of other metrics.

Executives should therefore have an early

choice of metrics that best fit the objectives of the 
machine learning AI project.
Recommendation 
3.2. 
Share 
the 
Responsibility for Evaluating the Performance 
of a Machine Learning System. Because the 
performance of a machine learning model is 
primarily evaluated by comparing its results 
against expected results, the evaluation is greatly 
affected by the validity of the expected results. 
Executives must therefore ensure the quality of 
expected results if they are to accurately evaluate 
the performance of a machine learning system. 
Moreover, because evaluation plays an important 
role in shaping the refinement of a machine 
learning model, it is also important to develop 
clear evaluation criteria with the development 
team early on. 
Recommendation 
3.3. 
Evaluate 
the 
Predictions Made by the AI System Through 
Cross-Validation. Data prepared by humans 
and predictions from the AI system should be 
cross-validated to ensure that the evaluation 
of the system’s performance is accurate and 
effective. After validation, any correction made 
to the training dataset can also be used in future 
training. Although the current trend, for good 
reasons, is for developers and users to try and 
understand why the machine learning AI model 
is wrong, sometimes the predictions can prompt 
forward-thinking 
organizations 
to 
critically 
evaluate their own knowledge and expertise. 
Executives in such organizations possess what 
we call “AI leadership competences.” Executives 
that truly want their businesses to benefit from 
machine learning AI have recognized that AI will 
augment the knowledge and expertise underlying 
their professional business contexts.
Recommendation 
3.4. 
Interpret 
the 
Predictions by Making Sense of Clues Rather 
than Seeking Explanations of the Reasoning. 
It is much harder to explain the behavior of a 
machine learning model, particularly a deep 
learning model, than it is for a rule-based system. 
Nevertheless, there are techniques32 that provide 
valuable clues that can help users make sense 
of how a machine learning AI system reaches

These tools enable executives who possess “AI

prepare for all of these to be augmented by 
machine learning AI.
Concluding Comments
Many organizations are currently assessing 
whether and how they might adopt machine 
learning AI. There is a long way to go before AI 
will routinely be capable of carrying out quasi-
human intellectual tasks, so developing machine 
learning AI systems that are specifically designed 
for domain-specific tasks is, at present, the most 
viable AI solution for organizations. However, as 
the LegalTechCo case demonstrates, developing a 
machine learning system can be very challenging 
and is vastly different from the development of 
traditional information systems. But the case also 
shows that a machine learning system can be 
developed successfully for knowledge-intensive 
work. Based on the experiences of LegalTechCo, 
we have provided actions and recommendations 
for addressing the challenges of developing 
machine learning AI systems for knowledge-
intensive work. These recommendations will also 
assist executives in developing what we call “AI 
leadership competences.”

This teaching case explores the challenges of changing a work system by implementing 
an information system (IS). The case describes the approach implemented by “The Bank”, 
a financial service provider, when it implemented a new financial and banking IS 
“SysOne”, and thus fundamentally changed its work systems. The case is a real business 
scenario, which bases on case study research conducted by our research team and it 
adapts recent theoretical advances in the IS implementation literature. Using this 
teaching case in class should encourage students to discuss IS implementations from a 
general “system thinking” rather than a “tool thinking” perspective. An IS 
implementation is not just a new tool, it is a change of employees’ work systems. This 
teaching case should guide students to extend the efforts implemented to guide employees 
when implementing an IS beyond the technology to focus on the major IT-induced work 
system changes and thereby enable successful technochange.  
Keywords: Change management, IS implementation, work system theory, user
