Introduction 
Managing information technology (IT)-induced change well in organizations has been one of the major 
concerns of CIOs over the past years (Luftman and Derksen 2012). This change typically involves 
implementing enterprise systems such as enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship 
management (CRM) or enterprise content management (ECM) systems, but also changes in employees’ 
usual routines, tasks, or workflows (Laumer et al. 2016; Volkoff et al. 2007). Implementing these 
information systems (IS) causes, at least, short-term inconveniences leading to user resistance behaviors 
(Kim and Kankanhalli 2009; Laumer et al. 2017; Lee and Joshi 2016) that are a major reason why 
organizational change initiatives fail altogether or do not meet the initial expectations (Klaus and Blanton 
2010; Lapointe and Rivard 2005; Nelson 2007). 
In this context, a major objective of change management is to communicate the advantages of the change 
to the employees. Many strategies and techniques for implementing an IS successfully have been proposed 
(Aladwani 2001; Sykes 2015). But most of these follow what Alter (2013) calls “tool thinking”, which focus 
on the IT driving the change rather than on the change induced by the implementation (Markus 2004). By 
doing so, these approaches neglect corresponding changes in business processes or other organizational 
elements (Morris and Venkatesh 2010; Volkoff et al. 2007) which might be an important reason for IS 
implementation failure (Nelson 2007). To avoid this mistake, recent theoretical approaches (e.g., Alter 
2013; Markus 2004) encourage more general “system thinking” (Alter 2013) to extend the focus beyond the 
technology and to include organizational elements when managing IT-induced work system changes.  
This teaching case provides a case study to teach students to shift from a “tool thinking” to a general “system 
thinking” approach (Alter 2013) when implementing an IS in an organization. The teaching case is based 
on a real-world implementation of a financial and banking information system at an SME financial service 
provider (Laumer et al. 2012). In the following, we introduce the theoretical background (work system 
theory, technochange, change management processes, user resistance) and the company, describe the 
implementation project, and provide the perspectives of several employees. This information is the basis 
for the class discussion. Teaching notes providing a structure for leading class discussions and helping 
students achieve learning goals are provided on request1.  
Theoretical background 
The teaching case is based on the work system theory and the technochange approach. Furthermore, the 
work system change approach is based on Kotter’s (1995) eight change management steps. The teaching 
case illustrates an IT-induced change of a work system that can be defined as an IT-enabled change of 
organizational elements (Gibson 2003) such as data, processes, working routines, structure, or culture 
(Laumer et al. 2016; Volkoff et al. 2007). Such IT-induced changes are caused by implementing an IS, and 
they have an impact on individual tasks, working routines, and organizational processes (Lapointe and 
Rivard 2005; Volkoff et al. 2007). The main management focus of IT-induced changes of work systems 
should be the people, as an IT-driven change induces “a change in the work behavior of people” (Gibson 
2003, p. 105). This section summarizes the theoretical ideas that focus on the people-side of IS 
implementations in organizations which are the basis for the teaching case. Students should be familiar 
with these concepts before analyzing and discussing the teaching case. Table 4 provides a reading list to get 
familiar with these concepts.  
Technochange 
The term technochange was introduced by Markus (2004) and describes a technology-driven 
organizational change initiative. The general objective of technochange initiatives is the “improvement in 
organizational performance” (Markus 2004, p. 5). In these types of projects, IS implementations are 
complemented by related organizational changes to achieve organizational performance with an 
appropriate fit between the system and the organization. Markus 2004 distinguishes technochange 
initiatives from typical IT projects, suggesting that the major risk factor in implementing IS in organizations

Work system theory 
A key theory underlying the teaching case is work system theory. The general objective of the work system 
theory is to follow a “system thinking” instead of a “tool thinking” approach when discussing, analyzing, 
developing or implementing IS in organizations. That is, rather than focusing on IS, work system theory 
focuses on work systems, defined as “a system in which human participants and/or machines perform 
work (processes and activities) using information, technology, and other resources to produce specific 
products/services for specific internal and/or external customers“ (Alter 2013, p. 75). The work system 
theory proposes an understanding of IS implementations that does not focus on the IT itself, but rather on 
the work system in which the IT is used by participants to perform their work activities. Hence, it provides 
the basis for analyzing and discussing IT-induced change, as the technology element of a work system might 
induce changes in the other elements such as information, work practices, products and services, or 
customers (Alter 2008) Figure 1 illustrates the work system framework according to Alter (2013).

Change management 
Kotter (1995) describes the process of any organizational change in eight phases. First, one needs to 
establish a sense of urgency. Everybody in the organization needs to be convinced that a change is necessary. 
Second, a powerful guiding coalition needs to be formed that leads the change process. Third, a vision needs 
to be created and, fourth, the vision needs to be communicated. Fifth, measures needs to be implemented 
to empower others to act on the vision. Sixth, it is important to plan for and create short-term wins. Seventh, 
it is necessary to consolidate improvements and to produce still more change. Finally, the new approach in 
the organization is institutionalized (Kotter 1995).

In addition to Kotter’s (1995) organizational view on the change management process Schwarz et al. (2014) 
provide five steps from an individual’s point of view. In the first phase, i.e. receive, the individual gets the 
information that a new IS is going to be implemented. In the second phase, grasp, the individual evaluates 
to what extent one is willing to intellectually comprehend the intentionality (e.g., functionality and design) 
of the new IS. In phase three, assess, individuals assess whether the new IS is valuable to oneself and the 
organization. In phase four, be given, the individual adapt one’s routines to the new IS and finally in phase 
five, submit, the individual is fully surrendered by the new IS. Figure 2 illustrate both process models of an 
IT-induced change.  
User resistance 
In the context of IS implementations, individuals often react with showing resistant behaviors. The five 
steps provided by Schwarz et al. (2014) propose a process model for understanding such employees’ 
reactions to an IS implementation. User resistance research in general explains why and how individuals 
resist IS implementations (Lee and Joshi 2016). This reaction is based psychologically at the individual level 
(Jermier et al. 1994) and is determined by perceptions about a new IS implementation or the changes 
related to it. Hence, a perceived threat about an aspect of an IS implementation determine user resistance 
behavior (Lapointe and Rivard 2005).  
Research has focused on several aspects of an IS implementation including the individual oneself (Laumer 
et al. 2015) or perceived threats related to the IS itself, the change from the status quo, work routines, the 
legacy system and the loss of power (Laumer et al. 2016; Lee and Joshi 2016). In terms of user resistance 
behavior it has been shown that this type of behavior can be overt (open and expressive) or covert 
(concealed or hidden), and can take an active (originating action) or a passive (inert or not acting) form 
(Kim and Kankanhalli 2009). Several behaviors are attributed as a user resistance behavior (Laumer et al. 
2017) including the non-use of the IS (Klaus and Blanton 2010) and also related behavior such as employee 
turnover (Maier et al. 2013), complaining (Klaus et al. 2010; Laumer et al. 2014), workarounds (Rivard and 
Lapointe 2012), and sabotage (Klaus et al. 2010).

Interviews 
In 2011, the external consultant visited the organization to gain a better understanding of the situation, its 
drivers and its consequences. The results of these interviews are presented in the following. First, the 
opinion of each employee on “SysOne” implementation is presented and afterwards those statements that 
describe the consequences are summarized. 
“SysOne” implementation 
The first employee interviewed was the project manager. He was the vice-project manager of “SysOne” 
implementation and was involved in both the pre-implementation and implementation efforts. He was also 
the main project manager for the merger that took place before “SysOne” was implemented. Hence, the 
project manager has experiences in organizational change projects and project management techniques in 
general. He summarizes the “SysOne” implementation and links the “SysOne” implementation to the 
overall change history of the organization:  
 “Our house has had to make many changes in the past years. First, there was the merger that 
raised existential fears for some of our employees, even though the corporate headquarters 
guaranteed there would be no layoffs. The merger caused a reorganization of our staff 
department and the employees were allocated to different executives. Then, a few years later a 
completely new financial and banking information system arrived that confronted our employees 
with lots of challenges. On the one hand, they could no longer rely on their acquired day-to-day 
experience and on the other hand the use of SysOne caused great uncertainty.

From a business perceptive, the marketing and sales director describes the “SysOne” implementation. 
Especially the sales employees were affected by the “SysOne” implementation as the new IS requires sales 
employees to work more with the system than they were used to with the legacy system. Therefore, the 
marketing and sales director was confronted with many employees complaining about “SysOne”, as he is 
the superior of sales representatives and counselors. Therefore, he is able to provide an overview of 
employees’ reactions to the “SysOne” implementation as follows:  
“My employees are burdened by a lot of work and the many changes from the past years are still 
annoying and exhausting them. The new system requires my employees in sales to spend much 
more time on administrative tasks so they have lost a considerable amount of time to spend on 
actual consulting. 
With the old application, we had fewer problems and also had a good strategy for using it: The 
operational department relieved the consultants of all organizational tasks, so they could spend 
their time extensively with customers. My employees were trained appropriately for the new 
system, for example using an online learning portal, but as we all know, the theoretical 
fundamentals differ completely from practical situations with the customers. 
In the meantime, my employees are satisfied with SysOne. I believe this is due to the outstanding 
work of our executives. However, they are less pleased with the new instructions, which take up 
a considerable amount of extra time from the single consultations. We have to do additional work, 
which has been done by other people previously. For example, sales representative have to do all 
administrative work like printing and sending contracts, which has been done by a sales assistant 
before the new system was implemented. With the new system, the focus is much more on cost 
and efficiency rather than on net sales time, even though net sales time is much more important

can completely understand my employees on these points, since I worked in operations, too, 
before I became marketing director and thus share their opinions. Unfortunately, I believe that 
the board does not even acknowledge these concerns.”

On these grounds, I am in close contact with the new process officer and with him I am trying to 
intensify and improve the work with the executives. 
The challenges for our employees were not just due to our merger. Our executives still have not 
attended our program and thus don’t know the underlying processes. Thus, they were and are 
not a helpful contact for our employees, which resulted in many issues in the process operation. 
Moreover, the information management was very poor. Changes were not specifically 
communicated to many employees. For this reason, there were many discrepancies. Nevertheless, 
we learned from our mistakes and are currently introducing information and quality 
management practices. In addition, our communication has to be reconsidered in order to better 
represent both the perceived benefits as well as the strains. Therefore, we are currently 
conducting an employee survey and hope for new insights in this area.” 
Consequences of “SysOne” implementation 
Beside the “SysOne” implementation and the consequences for individual working routines, the interviews 
also revealed several indications of additional consequences of the “SysOne” implementation, which are 
presented in the following.  
According to the sales and marketing director, the implementation of “SysOne” has an impact on three 
work-related indexes the organization is monitoring regularly: turnover behavior, job satisfaction, and 
commitment. The organization uses an annual survey to monitor these indexes, which reveals a higher 
turnover, lower job satisfaction and a lower continuous staff commitment after “SysOne”. The sales and 
marketing director mentioned explicitly: 
“In my department one of my better sales representatives left the organization as he felt totally 
unhappy with the new way of working.”  
In this context, another sales representative pointed out:

There is a need for case studies that provide opportunities to learn the difficult nuances of project management that 
are difficult to effectively recreate within another‟s mind.  This article offers survival skills in project management for 
the difficult existing business environment, particularly within information systems, of today.  The case study 
considers the tragic expeditions in 1996 to scale the peak of Mount Everest. Things went terribly wrong, ending in 
the deadliest tragedy in the history of the mountain.  The accounts of the survivors summarized within several books 
on the ordeal are used to consider the implications of project management issues that pervade such difficult projects  
–  leadership styles, hubris, planning, communication, and constraints.  Readers of this case study should consider 
effectively implementing practices that could prove to be the difference in surviving an “Everest” project. 
 
Keywords: teaching case, project management, pedagogy

I. INTRODUCTION 
“I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand.” 
                   - Confucius 551-479 BC 
To summit Mount Everest is one of the most coveted achievements in the realm of earth-bound exploration.  In 
1985, Texas businessman Dick Bass reached the summit of Everest at the relatively advanced age of 55.  The 
adventuresome and the wealthy took notice, setting their sights on this exceptional and unique accomplishment. 
Commercial expedition companies surfaced to exploit the demand as there was a significant number of customers 
eager to pay the steep fee for the chance to summit the world‟s highest peak.   
More than a decade later on May 10th, 1996, eight climbers would die on the slopes of Everest, including two of the 
most highly regarded commercial mountaineering guides in the world: Rob Hall and Scott Fischer. Two more 
climbers would lose limbs to frost-bite.  Later analysis would reveal that the year‟s summit attempt had taken too 
long; time ran out for the unfortunate climbers trapped on the mountain in severe weather and waning light. 
In contemporary business environments, time is often similarly highly constraining. Information systems projects in 
particular often exhibit characteristics of being “Everest projects” – those projects in which a combination of size and 
complexity leads to mistakes and failures that result in disaster. In the case of the Everest expedition of 1996, 
deteriorating weather, darkness, and dwindling oxygen plagued the climbers on their attempted descent.  It has 
been noted that “climbing today is not only mainstream, it is a business, and with that comes the rising tendency for 
climbing decisions – objectives as well as tactical decisions on a climb – to be business decisions as well” [Boukreev 
1997, pg. iv]. While not facing the same life or death consequences, the Everest tragedy provides an interesting 
context in which to develop an understanding of potentially devastating pitfalls that could apply equally well to major 
IS projects. 
II.  BACKGROUND 
In the early morning of May 10th, 1996, the two commercial expeditions of Hall and Fischer began their summit bid 
on Mount Everest.  New Zealander Rob Hall, 35 years old, headed the commercial expedition Adventure 
Consultants.  Hall began taking expeditions to Everest in 1990, and had achieved summiting a record 39 climbers to 
the top of Everest.  His company‟s advertisements touted „one hundred percent success” until May 1995, when he 
turned all of his clients back from their bid for the summit as deep snows at higher elevations had slowed their 
progress.  Business pressure intensified as Scott Fischer had entered into the competitive commercial expedition 
market with his company Mountain Madness.  Fischer had been successful in packaging expeditions to the remotest 
destinations in Africa, South America, and Asia, attracting customers from around the world. 
In an effort to generate press, Fischer and his staff looked for opportunities to gain media attention. Outside, the 
leading outdoor-recreation magazine in the United States, wanted to sponsor Jon Krakauer as a climber on one of 
Fischer‟s Everest expeditions. Krakauer was a Seattle-based journalist and best-selling author who would write a 
feature article on the boom in commercial expeditions to Mount Everest.  Outside wanted a significant discount for 
Krakauer‟s slot on Fischer‟s team.  At one point, Outside went to Rob Hall, who gave them a better deal and got 
Krakauer on his expedition.  Mountain Madness was successful in signing on Sandy Pittman, a Contributing Editor 
to Allure and Conde Nast Traveler magazines.  She also offered media exposure through an agreement with NBC 
interactive Media to do a daily feed to a web site [Boukreev 1997].  The media coverage represented an opportunity 
for both expedition companies but also raised the stakes, as success - or failure - would be reported around the 
world.  
That year, more than 400 people eventually ended up at Everest Base Camp.  One climber described the 
encampment as having all the appearances of “a circus, except there were more clowns in our tents.”  By many 
accounts there were expeditions planning to summit Everest without the experience or guidance that would usually 
be found on a team [Boukreev 1997;Krakauer 1997]. 
The summit bid offered by the two commercial expeditions followed a standard routine of spending approximately 
one month acclimatizing to the thin air associated with high altitudes.  Sherpas would progressively establish a 
series of four camps above Base Camp.  Food, cooking fuel, and oxygen would be moved from camp to camp until 
 
 
Volume 24 
Article 44 
779 
the requisite material was at 26,000 feet on the South Col and the climbers had been adequately acclimatized.  
From Camp IV, the final push would be made to the summit of Mount Everest. 
While the two commercial expeditions of Rob Hall and Scott Fischer are the focus of this case study, three additional 
expeditions were either part of, or gave a unique perspective to, the tragedy that would unfold.  Although they had 
promised not to make a summit bid on the same day as Hall and Fischer, Taiwanese and South African 
noncommercial expeditions also completed the final leg of the summit on May 10th.  By all accounts, the Taiwanese 
and South African expeditions were high risk because both teams lacked qualifications and experience.  The third 
party was the IMAX/IWERKS filming expedition led by David Brashears.  Brashears, an exceptional climber, led this 
expedition to summit Mount Everest and complete filming the journey on May 9th.  Having concerns about the 
weather and the unusually large group of climber‟s planning to summit on May 10th, his party decided to descend 
and summit later.  He offers an expert‟s perspective from outside the expeditions that were to summit on May 10th. 
III. PROBLEMS SUGGESTED BY PROJECT MANAGEMENT 
Project management has emerged as a core competence within business domains, particularly information systems. 
It offers a useful lens through which to evaluate how such endeavors can meet the competing demands of time, 
cost, quality and scope while balancing the needs and expectations of various stakeholders.   Five issues 
consistently surface as the most significant from a project management perspective – leadership styles, hubris, 
planning, communication, and constraints.  Although the challenges in these domains are discussed herein 
separately, they are not independent.  Rather, they overlap, interact and compound with each other in complicated 
ways.   And while these interactions are not discussed within the case, it is important for the reader to consider the 
relationships and their impact on the project.  
This case study utilizes “A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge” (PMBOK® Guide) developed by 
the Project Management Institute [Institute 1996; Institute 2000; Institute 2004] as a framework for contemplating the 
issues raised by the doomed Everest expeditions of 1996.  The PMBOK provides a framework of processes that are 
generally recognized as good practice for project management [Institute 2004].  It is the foundation for the project 
management professional certification and an ANSI and ISO standard.  In addition to the PMBOK, the Theory of 
Constraints (TOC) [Goldratt 1987;Goldratt 1997]  will be utilized to offer insights and learning opportunities into the 
Mount Everest tragedy.   
Issue 1: Leadership styles 
Hall and Fischer made for an interesting contrast in leadership styles.  Brashears notes that Fischer‟s “leadership 
style exhibited great faith in the human spirit as if to say to clients, I‟m not going to hold your hand all the way, I‟m 
not going to map it out for you, there‟s something in this experience for you to sort out on your own” [Breashears 
2000, pg. 240].  This was in stark contrast to the rule-based approach taken by Rob Hall.  Boukreev and DeWalt 
summarize the differences, stating:  
The difference between Hall’s and Fischer’s philosophies of guiding are emblematic of an ongoing debate 
between practitioners in the adventure travel industry.  The camps of belief can be roughly divided between 
the ‘situationalists’ (Scott’s style) and the ‘legalists,’ (Rob’ style).  The situationalists argue that in leading a 
risky adventure, no rules can adequately cover every situation that may arise, and they argue that rules on 
some occasions should be subordinated to unique demands that present themselves.  The legalists, 
believing that rules can substantially reduce the possibility of bad decisions being made, ask that personal 
freedom take a backseat. [Boukreev 1997, pg. 155] 
As a legalist, Hall tightly controlled the climb and left little to the determination of the clients. For example, 
acclimatization was completed as a group. All members were asked to stick together as they went from camp to 
camp the first several weeks.  As a situationalist, Fischer felt acclimatization was unique to each climber.  “Even 
though Boukreev and Fischer hoped to move the clients through it together, they understood there would be varying 
response to their recommended routine and tried to build some flexibility into the regimen” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 72].  
Boukreev explains further,  “personally, I looked with concern upon the closely regimented expeditions where clients 
performed as tin soldiers.  Given my history as a trainer and coach in cross-country skiing and mountaineering, I felt 
it was important to encourage independent action” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 106]. 
Hall‟s leadership style and mandated rules became constraints just as potent as any physical one. This proved 
costly to all the expeditions on the mountain that fateful day; their summit bids became intertwined and impacted the 
climb durations for everyone.  Krakauer explains, “Hall had instructed the climbers for the first half of the summit day 
not to put any more than 100 meters between themselves until they reached the Balcony, a cleft at the base of the 
Southeast Ridge at about 8,500 meters” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 154; Krakauer 1997, pg. 174]. Krakauer, accustomed 
 
 
780 
Volume 24 
Article 44 
to independence of action as a climber, was “frustrated at having his decisions tied to the lowest common 
denominators of the climb” [Krakauer 1997, pg. 154], but he felt his position as client forced him to give up his 
personal commitment to self-reliance and independent decision-making, to become a “tin soldier.”  In his book, 
Krakauer writes “passivity on the part of the clients has thus become encouraged throughout the expedition” 
[Krakauer 1997, pg. 176]. Accordingly, Krakauer and Ang Dorje (Sherpa), after stop-and-go progress that had cost 
them more than an hour, reached the Balcony, stopped and sat down on their backpacks not advancing any higher. 
Were it not for Hall‟s rigid rules, they would have been preparing the fixed ropes and climbing towards the summit. 
Ironically, Hall hedged at setting a specific turnaround time for the summit attempt – a proven critical success factor 
in extreme mountaineering. Whether or not the summit has been achieved, failure to begin a descent at or before a 
predetermined turnaround time has led to multiple deaths on the world‟s tallest peaks. Brashears commented “It was 
none of our business what Hall and Fischer had decreed as their turnaround time, but we knew they would have one 
and that it was probably one or two o‟clock.  That would leave only a window of 30 – 90 minutes for their clients to 
finish the climb … but, at three p.m. we looked up and could see climbers still forging across the traverse to the 
Hillary Step.  Ed (another climbing expert) and I were alarmed … Before our eyes, we could see people willfully 
giving away their small margin of safety for success on the summit.  What they were sacrificing was the ability to 
return to Camp IV in the safety of daylight.  It can‟t be overstated how light provides an asylum up there.  Light gives 
you more than just vision and the ability to see your path or the promise of a camp down below.  It fundamentally 
binds your morale; that‟s what they were giving away.  Night creates a different mountain.  Unless you‟ve managed 
to memorize the labyrinth, really gathered the landmarks into your mind, you can be lost in an instant” [Breashears 
2000, pg. 261]. 
Issue 1: Questions to Consider 
1. 
What are the advantages and disadvantages of the different leadership styles considering this situation? 
2. 
Considering the use of formal and informal control mechanisms, would one leadership style be more 
prone to use formal versus informal? 
3. 
By which style and control mechanisms would you rather be managed? 
Issue 2: Hubris 
Hubris is exaggerated pride, self-confidence, or arrogance, frequently resulting in retribution. As he climbed the 
mountain after the catastrophe, Brashears recounts seeing the corpse of Rob Hall: “mingled with my sorrow I must 
confess, were feelings of anger toward Rob … I knew in my bones that the mistakes made May 10th could have 
been avoided, that hubris had likely doomed Rob and his party. Of all the guides, Rob had been most outspoken 
about his prowess, and the most proprietary about the mountain.  He had sometimes acted as if he were a part-
owner of Everest, an attitude I found disturbing” [Breashears 2000, pg. 27]. 
Other accounts further suggest hubris in both leaders. For example, Gammelgard, a client of the Mountain Madness 
expedition, thought people had an unrealistic image of Fischer that he felt he had to maintain.  She offers, “It was 
really shocking to see in Pakistan that the people who were on the support trek, the only thing they could see was 
their image of a hero. They just couldn‟t see the human being.  They just absolutely were totally blind to the reality.  
They had that picture of what a hero should be, and they addressed him like that, but they couldn‟t see him” 
[Boukreev 1997, pg. 32]. 
Jon Krakauer confirmed the impact of hubris when he reflected on the essential reasons for the tragedy, noting that 
“hubris probably had something to do with it. Hall had become so adept at running climbers of all abilities up and 
down Everest that he got a little cocky, perhaps. He'd bragged on more than one occasion that he could get almost 
any reasonably fit person to the summit, and his record seemed to support this. He'd also demonstrated a 
remarkable ability to prevail over adversity…” [Krakauer 1997, pg. 284-285]. 
Certainly time had as much to do with the tragedy as the weather, and ignoring the clock cannot be passed off as an 
act of God. Delays at critical points in the ascent were foreseeable and eminently preventable. Predetermined 
turnaround times were egregiously ignored.  Extending the turnaround times may have been influenced to some 
degree by the rivalry between Fischer and HaIl.  Fischer had never guided Everest before 1996.  From a business 
perspective, there was tremendous pressure on Fischer to be successful in that climbing season.  He was 
exceedingly motivated to get clients to the summit - especially a celebrity client like Sandy Hill Pittman. 
Likewise, since he had failed to get any clients to the summit of Everest in 1995, it would have been bad for Hall's 
business if he failed again in 1996 – especially if Fischer succeeded.  “Fischer had a charismatic personality, and 
that charisma had been aggressively marketed. Fischer was trying very hard to be viewed as the premier 
mountaineering guide and Hall knew it.  Under the circumstances, the prospect· of turning his clients around while

his rival's clients were pushing toward the summit may have been sufficiently distasteful to cloud Hall's judgment” 
[Krakauer 1997, pg. 284-285]. 
Issue 2: Questions to Consider 
1. 
Many of the climbing guides subordinate to Fischer and Hall were new to the teams.  Did this have an 
impact? 
2. 
What actions could have been taken to reduce the impact of hubris? 
 
Issue 3: Planning and considering risk 
“If expeditions are not adequately provisioned when the time for their summit bid arrives, they might as well have 
never traveled to the mountain” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 3].  Indeed, there is a multitude of details associated with the 
logistics of moving that much equipment, food, materials and people in a remote part of the world.  A key part of 
planning for summit attempts concerns ensuring adequate oxygen supplies for the summit bid.  Atmospheric oxygen 
levels are so low at and above Camp IV that the majority of climbers use bottled oxygen to sustain brain and bodily 
functions and, ultimately, to survive.    
Given how they intended to use it, the quantity of oxygen available to the Mountain Madness expedition at Camp IV 
was minimal.  The oxygen consumption/use calculations upon which Fischer based his oxygen plan was in part 
based upon advice from his supplier Henry Todd.  Todd estimated that each of his canisters, if consumed at his 
suggested flow rate of 2 to 2.5 liters/minute, would last for 6 hours.  “Two should last you for twelve hours, and that 
12 hours should take you to the summit (from Camp IV) and then back down to pick up a third bottle at the South 
Summit. On paper the plan looked bulletproof” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 151].   However, this assumed everything would 
proceed according to plan.  It further assumed that no additional oxygen would be needed for those stricken with 
HACE (High Altitude Cerebral Edema, or swelling of the brain, a condition associated with oxygen depletion), for 
those older climbers who require more oxygen to keep warm, or for any other unforeseen event or condition that 
could slow the pace of climbing. 
Issue 3: Questions to Consider 
1. 
Consider this issue and a) identify risks, b) prioritize these risks, and c) come up with appropriate risk 
responses for those with potentially high impact and high probability. 
2. 
One option for addressing risk is to place buffer or contingency at the end of the phase or project.  Would 
this have helped? 
3. 
The clientele had paid significant sums of money to summit Everest.  Should they have been made aware 
of the assumptions made in the plan to summit?  Whose risk was it? 
Issue 4: Communications 
An essential process within any project is effective and efficient communication. Unfortunately, there were serious 
communication breakdowns during the 1996 expeditions, especially within the Mountain Madness team.  In his 
recount of the tragedy, Boukreev admitted, “communication was a huge problem … a problem I failed to completely 
appreciate until it was too late” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 267]. 
Concerning communication technology, “…there were equipment issues, and one concern that arose early was that 
of the two-way radios Fischer had brought for use by the expedition.  A critical item in an expedition inventory, a 
radio creates a link between Base Camp and climbers as they wind their way to the summit and provides a conduit 
for information on developing problems, emergencies, equipment needs, the weather, and medical matters.  An 
experienced climber considers the state of his expedition‟s communications capabilities, and Martin Adams did.  
“These days you have these great little radios that weigh next to nothing that every one of the climbers should have, 
because the cost of carrying them is zero.  They‟re easy to use - two buttons - it‟s black and white.  And Scott pulls 
out a few of these old radios with ten channels and I said, „These are the radios we‟re using?‟  And he says to me, 
„Yeah, this is all I got.‟  The radios, in my opinion, were a joke.  It was a major misstep for him to go over there with 
these antiquated models” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 70]. 
The lack of communication proved costly as none of the guides could communicate with Fischer as the group 
climbed the mountain.  Boukreev explains, “I was on the summit about an hour.  I had no radio, nor did Neal, so 
neither of us knew what was going on below.  I suspected there might be trouble at the Hillary Step, and I felt I 
should go down.  At about 2:00 PM, maybe slightly later, I moved away from the summit…” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 
173]. However, his skills might have been better utilized ushering clients up the summit. 
 
 
782 
Volume 24 
Article 44 
Another communication barrier was the differences in language and culture.   Boukreev was Russian and felt 
stymied by the language differences.  As he noted, “… my English left much to be desired and I couldn‟t always 
freely answer their questions and vice versa.  I couldn‟t take the initiative and advise something practical like a guide 
is supposed to explain the importance of my advice” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 82]. 
Finally, poor communication hindered decision making and had guides questioning one another‟s authority and roles 
on the mountain.  Both expeditions were depending on the guide services of men who had never climbed Everest.  
This limited experience made them uncomfortable offering opinions or challenging decisions that were made.  The 
Mountain Madness expedition had retained the services of Boukreev, who possessed tremendous depth of 
experience but who also felt shut out of the decision making process.  Boukreev explained, “I wanted very much for 
my feelings to be heard, but it had become increasingly clear to me that Scott did not look upon my advice in the 
same way as he did Rob Hall‟s ... My voice was not as authoritative as I would have liked, so I tried not to be 
argumentative, choosing instead to downplay my intuitions” [Boukreev 1997, pg. 140]. 
Issue 4: Questions to Consider 
1. 
Considering the importance of the communication technology, how could such a decision be made? 
2. 
Considering this issue, are there any tools and techniques that could have mitigated the communication 
issues? 
3. 
Boukreev was hired because he was one of the best climbers in the world.  Was that sufficient to make 
the hiring decision?  If not, what else should have been considered? 
Issue 5: Constraints 
The physical constraints presented by Mount Everest pose serious challenges at every turn when making a summit 
bid.  “Expeditions now arrive and find themselves in immediate competition for such basic resources as flat tent 
sites.  In 1996 there were ten Everest expeditions needing space on a thin slice of the Khumbu Glacier” [Breashears 
2000, pg. 231].  Negotiations by Hall and Fischer with the other expeditions provided Adventure Consultants and 
Mountain Madness the opportunity to summit on their preferred date of May 10th.  Concerned about the size of their 
parties, the two expeditions wanted to summit alone.  The Taiwanese and South African expeditions, however, 
wanted to draft on the expertise of the commercial expeditions and planned to summit on May 10th also, even 
though they had agreed not to do this in earlier negotiations. 
The physical constraints of the climb ultimately would manifest in three important ways.  First, the sheer limitations of 
the mountain strain every capacity with so many people attempting to summit. Breashears was above the two 
commercial expeditions when they were making their way to Camp IV.  As Breashears was descending because of 
deteriorating weather, he noted, “We all agreed – none of us had ever seen so many people hunched so close 
together, hanging from the same ropes … I could imagine the traffic jam that would ensue.  People going up would 
meet people going down, all trying to use the same rope.  Each time, someone would have to unclip to get around 
someone else, then clip in again – time-consuming and dangerous work.  I knew from experience that there isn‟t 
strength in numbers on Everest” [Breashears 2000, pgs. 252 and 256]. 
A second constraint was the need for fixed ropes above Camp IV.  The ropes were not in place as planned when the 
expedition arrived, causing inordinate delays in the summit bid.  Consequently, the climbers experienced a traffic jam 
at the base of the Hillary Step when a dozen or more climbers came to a standstill waiting in queue as the ropes 
were anchored and then used by the assembled climbers.  A single rope was placed, causing delays and dangerous 
work, just as envisioned by Brashears.  In his popular book, Jon Krakauer would describe the sheer horror of 
standing at the top of the Hillary Step while his oxygen ran out, unable to descend because of the other climbers 
coming up the fixed rope for over an hour. 
The third physical constraint surfaced as the two teams of differing abilities intermingled.  The colloquialism “a team 
is only as strong as the weakest member” offers significant insights into the compounding effect of the teams on 
Everest that fateful climb.  This was further exacerbated as the commercial expeditions, with their own limitations, 
were joined by the even weaker Taiwanese and South African expeditions.  This lethal mixture of strong and weak 
talent began taking its considerable toll when a member of the Taiwanese expedition used the bathroom without 
wearing ice crampons, slipped and slid into a deep crevasse.  Sherpas from the two commercial expeditions assisted 
the efforts to extricate the climber [Boukreev 1997].  Efforts to save his life consumed the limited reserve of the 
Sherpas‟ physical strength and dwindling oxygen supply.  Ultimately the climber perished.   
Commingling stronger with weaker climbers took an additional toll. Boukreev, an experienced climber and guide for 
the Mountain Madness expedition, worried about teaming up with the slower, less qualified Adventure Consultants 
expedition.  He felt that joining forces with the slower, less able team would hinder their climb [Boukreev 1997].  His 
 
 
Volume 24 
Article 44 
783 
concerns proved prophetic.  Rob Hall‟s slower team began first with a thirty minute head start.  Within two or three 
hours, the Mountain Madness climbers began to overtake Rob‟s climbers, and soon the teams were thoroughly 
fused along with three members of the Taiwanese Expedition.  Rob‟s clients in front of the faster climbers slowed the 
faster climbers as they couldn‟t pass.  This squandered precious time and oxygen and added to the traffic jam high 
on the world‟s tallest mountain. 
Issue 5: Questions to Consider 
1. 
Which of these physical constraints was the most constricting? 
2. 
Give solutions to each of these constraints. 
 
IV. CONCLUSION 
In considering the terrible personal tragedies that unfolded on Mount Everest in May 1996, we have sought to 
evaluate the role of project management in such endeavors. We believe that the poignancy of the Everest tragedies 
brings into sharp focus some important, though often difficult to discern, critical success factors on highly challenging 
projects. Indeed, many corporate projects, while perhaps not exposing people to a life threatening situation, might 
reasonably be termed “Everest” projects for their important similarities to what happened on the mountain in 1996.  
Still, Jon Krakauer offers an important warning :  
Analyzing what went wrong on Everest is a useful enough enterprise; it might conceivably prevent some 
deaths down the road.  But to believe that dissecting the tragic events of 1996 in minute detail will actually 
reduce the future death rate in any meaningful way is wishful thinking.  The urge to catalog the myriad of 
blunders in order to ‘learn from the mistakes’ is for the most part an exercise in denial and self-deception.  If 
you can convince yourself that Rob Hall died because he made a string of stupid errors and that you are too 
clever to repeat those same errors, it makes it easier for you to attempt Everest in the face of some rather 
compelling evidence that doing so is injudicious. [Krakauer 1997, pg. 284-285] 
 
In conclusion, to fall into the trap Krakauer details above shows that very little about the five issues addressed was 
actually understood on Everest in May 1996. How might history have been different had they been? 
Conclusion: Questions to Consider 
1. 
Which of these issues was the most important and should have been considered first? 
2. 
How did these issues interplay: leadership styles, hubris, planning, communication, and constraints? 
3. 
Can you eliminate or mitigate any one of these in isolation?  Do the issues need to be considered 
together?

b) A consulting team is preparing a client presentation under time pressure. The 
team consists of four members working from different locations and partly 
across time zones. They use Microsoft Teams for chat-based communication, 
email for external communication, and a shared PowerPoint file stored in 
SharePoint. The project lead assigns tasks via a Teams message, asking one 
team member to update numerical data and another to revise the slide design. 
The instructions refer to “the current version” and “the latest numbers.” 
During the day, team members work at different times. One team member 
edits the shared presentation directly in SharePoint, while another downloads a 
local copy, edits it offline, and later uploads it again. As a result, multiple 
versions of the presentation are worked on and later merged. At the same 
time, feedback from the client is communicated via email, stating that “they 
do not like it.” This information is not further specified, and clarification is 
delayed due to differing schedules and communication channels. When 
reviewing the presentation the next day, the project lead notices that 
numerical values differ across slides, layouts have changed, and comments in 
the document refer to elements such as “this chart” or “that version.” It is also 
not immediately visible who made which changes or whether all updates have 
been incorporated. 
Analyze the scenario using the 3C framework. For each dimension (i.e., 
communication, coordination, cooperation),  
• identify the key problems in this scenario 
• explain which groupware issues underlie them, and 
• explain how these problems affect the other dimensions.  
 
c) Briefly explain the role of awareness in the model. Propose one concrete 
strategy that directly address the relevant types of awareness in the scenario. 
• Explain how and why the strategy improves which type of awareness 
• Explain how this leads to improvements in communication, coordination, 
and cooperation. (7 points)

communication is defined in Media Richness Theory. To do so, include the role

Criteria 
Points 
Relevant Aspects

communication 
2 
Communication is a process within which a 
communicator (sender) sends a message, which is 
encoded into linguistic or non-linguistic signs, through 
specific communication channels to a communicant 
(receiver), who decodes it. (0.5 points for each bold 
keyword) 
Definition from slide 6 would also count (or mix of

communication 
6

equivocality.  (1 point)

Messages with a high degree of equivocality

Choosing a medium with low richness risks

Question 3: Digital Collaboration (30 Points) 
a) Describe the 3C’s of collaboration and how they relate to each other. 
Afterwards, define individual work including the two individual working modes, 
and explain its role and importance as part of collaborative work. (8 Points) 
Criteria 
Points 
Relevant Aspects 
C1: 3C’s of 
collaboration 
4 
- Communication: mutual exchange and understanding 
of several person among each other; includes 
information exchanges, messaging etc. (1) 
- Coordination: organization of task-related activities 
that must be carried out as part of group work; 
includes alignment of activities, scheduling, 
managing of dependencies (e.g., of tasks) (1) 
- Collaboration and cooperation: joint processing of 
objects (e.g., texts) in group work (collaboration), 
where there are common goals and joint 
responsibility for results (cooperation); refers to the 
work on shared goals and objects (1) 
- Relationship among the 3Cs: Communication as the 
basis for coordination and, coordination and 
communication as basis for collaboration; (1) 
C2: Individual work as 
part of collaborative 
work 
4 
- 
Individual work: tasks such as reading writing, 
thinking, and synthesizing information into internal 
knowledge structures that are done uninterrupted in 
solitude with no interruptions (1) 
• 
Types of individual work: deep work and shallow 
work (not required) 
- Deep Work: work performed in a distraction-free 
environment that require high levels of 
concentration and high cognitive resources; is 
needed to make progress on a task (1) 
- Shallow Work: non-cognitively demanding work such 
as sorting documents or scheduling meetings; may be 
performed while being distracted (1) 
- Individual work is a complementary part of 
collaborative work (1) 
• 
Collaborative work evolves in series of episodes 
with high interdependences and episodes where 
individual work is done on separate tasks.  
• 
Rhythm of collaboration: alternating between 
collaborative and individual work is key to 
produce effective work outcomes 
 
b) A consulting team is preparing a client presentation under time pressure. The 
team consists of four members working from different locations and partly 
across time zones. They use Microsoft Teams for chat-based communication, 
email for external communication, and a shared PowerPoint file stored in 
SharePoint. The project lead assigns tasks via a Teams message, asking one 
team member to update numerical data and another to revise the slide design. 
 
12 
The instructions refer to “the current version” and “the latest numbers.” 
During the day, team members work at different times. One team member 
edits the shared presentation directly in SharePoint, while another downloads a 
local copy, edits it offline, and later uploads it again. As a result, multiple 
versions of the presentation are worked on and later merged. At the same 
time, feedback from the client is communicated via email, stating that “they 
do not like it.” This information is not further specified, and clarification is 
delayed due to differing schedules and communication channels. When 
reviewing the presentation the next day, the project lead notices that 
numerical values differ across slides, layouts have changed, and comments in 
the document refer to elements such as “this chart” or “that version.” It is also 
not immediately visible who made which changes or whether all updates have 
been incorporated. 
Analyze the scenario using the 3C framework. For each dimension (i.e., 
communication, coordination, cooperation),  
• identify the key problems in this scenario 
• explain one groupware issue that underlies them, and 
• explain how these problems affect the other dimensions. (15 points) 
Criteria 
Points 
Relevant Aspects 
C1: Communication 
5 
Key Problem (shared understanding): Ambiguous 
references such as “the current version”, “the latest 
numbers”, or “they don’t like it” make it difficult for 
team members to interpret them (1) 
Groupware issue (2):  
• 
Context: i.e., shared understanding needed to 
interpret messages. In digital collaboration, 
utterances are often ambiguous and require 
both conversational and situational context. (1) 
Here: team members do not share a clear 
understanding of which version or content is 
being discussed, leading to misinterpretations. 
(1) 
• 
Deixis, i.e., Deictic expressions such as “this,” 
“that,” or “it” rely on a shared situational 
context. In distributed, asynchronous settings, 
this context is often missing, making such 
references unclear. 
These communication problems affect 
• 
Coordination, because unclear messages make it 
difficult to align tasks and responsibilities (1) 
• 
Cooperation, because misunderstandings about 
content lead to incorrect or inconsistent 
contributions to the shared artifact (1) 
C2: Coordination 
5 
Key Problem (alignment of work): lack of alignment in 
how tasks and activities are organized. Tasks are 
 
13 
assigned without precise references, and team members 
work asynchronously without clear synchronization. 
Groupware issue: 
• 
Synchronization, i.e., maintaining uniformity 
during synchronous use in shared documents such 
that participants see changes (1). Here: Team 
members work on the same task at different 
times and in different document versions without 
proper alignment mechanisms. As a result, 
updates are not coordinated, and work is 
duplicated or overwritten. (1) 
• 
Lack of group awareness, i.e., knowledge about 
who is doing what and when (1). Here: Team 
members are unaware of each other’s activities, 
leading to overlapping or conflicting work. 
These problems affect 
• 
Communication, because misunderstandings arise 
that require more communication (1) 
• 
Cooperation breaks down, since contributions are 
not properly aligned in the shared artifact (1) 
C3: Cooperation 
5 
Key Problem (joint execution of tasks): Cooperation 
problems become visible in the joint creation of the 
presentation. Multiple versions of the file are created 
and later merged, resulting in inconsistent data and 
design changes. 
Groupware issue:  
• 
Workspace awareness issues, i.e., understanding 
how a shared artifact is evolving and who has 
contributed what. In this case, it is unclear which 
version is current and which changes have been 
incorporated. 
These cooperation problems affect: 
• 
Communication, because inconsistencies require 
additional explanation and clarification 
• 
Coordination, because the team cannot reliably 
build on each other’s work 
 
c) Briefly explain the role of awareness in the model. Propose one concrete 
strategy that directly address the relevant types of awareness in the 
scenario. 
• Explain how and why the strategy improves which type of awareness 
• Explain how this leads to improvements in communication, coordination, 
and cooperation. (7 points) 
 
14 
C1: Role of awareness 
in the model 
2 
Awareness refers to an understanding of the activities of 
others and the state of shared work, which provides the 
context necessary for effective collaboration. In the 3C 
model, awareness is not a separate dimension but a 
mechanism that supports communication, coordination, 
and 
cooperation. 
When 
awareness 
is 
lacking, 
misunderstandings, misalignment, and inconsistencies 
arise. 
Strategy and type of 
awareness 
2 
Introduce real-time co-editing in the shared PowerPoint 
file combined with change tracking and version history, 
and enforce the use of the shared document instead of 
offline versions. (1) 
Workspace awareness: Real-time editing and change 
tracking make visible which parts of the document have 
been modified, who made specific changes, and which 
version ist he most current. (1) 
Effects on 3Cs 
3 
Communication: Improved awareness provides a shared 
context for interpreting messages. Since changes and 
their locations are visible, ambiguous references (e.g., 
“this version” or “that slide”) are reduced, making 
communication more precise and easier to understand. 
Coordination: Awareness of who is working on what and 
which changes have been made enables team members 
to align their activities. This reduces overlapping work 
and prevents conflicts, improving the coordination of 
tasks across time and individuals. 
Cooperation: Improved workspace awareness ensures 
that all team members work on the same, up-to-date 
version of the document. This allows contributions to be 
consistently integrated into a coherent shared artifact, 
avoiding inconsistencies and supporting effective joint 
work.

Question 1: Agility (30 Points) 
a) Please explain (do not just name!) the differences between plan-based 
(traditional) and agile software development methods based on three criteria 
of your choice. (6 Points) 
 
b) Imagine you receive a call from the management of a medium-sized company 
that seeks your advice as an IT consultant. The company builds sensors to 
surveil the characteristics of fluids, such as water, in tanks (e.g., temperature, 
concentration, oxygen level, etc.) and sells these sensors to other businesses. 
To control the sensors and to collect the data from the sensors, the company 
provides its customers with a software application. This application has been 
developed and is maintained by an in-house IT department comprising a team 
of six people: 
• Donatella is a well-experienced software engineer and has been the 
head of the team for five years now. She knows the history of the 
software that the team develops very well. 
• Leandro is the expert for the IT infrastructure and database 
architecture in the team. He is very reliable but not very 
communicative, as he prefers to focus on his tasks once they have 
been defined. 
• Bernardo is the most senior person in the team. Everybody likes him 
for his positivity and humor. However, his code contributions 
oftentimes contain some bugs because he is not very fluent in the 
most recent programming languages the team uses. 
• Giorgia is the team member with the most-developed coding skills. In 
her spare time, she engages in ethical hacking and has won several 
cyber security competitions. 
• Emilio is the apprentice in the team which he joined one year ago. He 
is a fast learner and sometimes provides suggestions to implement 
new techniques that he has learned about in vocational school, which 
he must visit every second month. 
• Alice has a lot of expertise in software testing and documentation. 
Her ability to find almost every bug sometimes annoys the other team 
members, but everybody is happy that she is part of the team and 
makes sure the customers receive a mostly flawless software. 
So far, the team has been able to deliver a smoothly running software using the 
waterfall method for its development. Every two years, the company releases a 
new software version, offering maintenance for prior versions in-between. 
However, new demands for the software emerge increasingly fast. Customers, 
 
2 
for instance, ask for the possibility to integrate the software in their cloud 
computing ecosystems and the government has just released new IT security 
requirements that the software must fulfill in the future. 
Because new or changing requirements emerge more frequently, the IT 
department is unsure whether it can proceed using the waterfall method. One 
team member has heard about an alternative method called Scrum, without 
knowing much about it. Therefore, the company asks you to lay out how they 
may apply Scrum. 
In response to this request, please do the following (14 Points): 
i) 
Provide a suggestion, which team member could take over which scrum 
role (i.e., product owner, scrum master, and development/agile team). 
Justify your answer. (5 points) 
ii) 
Based on your answer in i), describe shortly how the scrum flow 
(consisting of the phases pre-game/pre-sprint, development/sprint, and 
post-game/post-sprint) could look like at this company. Please do NOT 
focus on the details of the various meetings but lay out who does what in 
which phase. (9 Points) 
 
c) In the lecture, you learned that agility requires an agile mindset and that 
890ßmploying agile methods (“doing” agile) is not equivalent to “being” agile. 
On the other hand, one of our guest lecturers argued that using single agile 
practices can be beneficial even if an organization lacks an agile mindset. 
Please discuss the pros and cons of applying agile practices in non-agile work 
environments. Based on your arguments, conclude whether organizations 
should necessarily strive for “being” agile when applying agile practices.      
(10 Points) 
 
 
3 
Question 2: AI at the Workplace (30 Points) 
a) Define and explain the two concepts of automation and augmentation. Please 
also name and explain the different forms of augmentation. How does 
augmentation relate to automation? (10 Points) 
 
b) Imagine you are an IT project manager working in a company that develops 
security systems. To support the software developers in their tasks, the CDO of 
the company has decided to buy a subscription for Github’s Copilot for all 
software developers in the company. 
GitHub Copilot is an AI-powered code completion tool. It assists developers by 
suggesting code snippets, functions, and even entire lines or blocks of code 
directly within their integrated development environment (IDE) (e.g Visual 
Studio). Here are some of its key features: 
• Code Suggestions: Offers real-time code suggestions as you type, helping to 
speed up the coding process and reduce repetitive work. 
• Code Completion: Completes entire lines or blocks of code based on the 
context and the patterns it has learned from the vast amount of code it has 
been trained on. 
• Function Recommendations: Suggests complete functions, including input 
parameters and documentation comments, based on the function's name and 
context. 
• Multi-language Support: Supports a wide range of programming languages, 
making it versatile for various development projects. 
• Documentation and Comments: Generates comments and documentation for 
the code, which can help in understanding and maintaining the codebase. 
• Refactoring Assistance: Helps in refactoring code by suggesting improved 
ways to write existing code, enhancing readability and performance. 
• Test Case Generation: Can suggest test cases based on the code written, 
aiding in more comprehensive testing practices. 
You will be responsible for developing guidelines for the internal use of GitHub 
Copilot, which also determine which of the features become available for the 
developers. Developing security systems requires specific attention to ensuring 
code quality and data privacy, as well as avoiding flaws and biases. The 
guidelines should ensure the appropriate and risk-free use of GitHub Copilot in 
this setting. 
From the lecture, you recall that different configurations between humans and 
AI systems are possible:  
• Decision Support 
• AI in the Loop 
• Human-AI Collaboration and Teams 
• Human in the Loop 
• Full Delegation to AI 
 
4 
For each of the five configurations named above, please lay out how the 
interplay between Copilot and the developers could look and use selected 
features from above to illustrate your answers. Building on this analysis, please 
argue which configuration is most appropriate in the situation described. 
Additionally, decide which features the company should unlock for its 
developers and which not. Justify your answer. (15 points)  
 
c) Your team has recently started using GitHub Copilot to assist with code 
writing and completion tasks. While Copilot has significantly improved 
productivity, there have been instances where developers have heavily relied 
on its suggestions without critically evaluating them. This is especially a 
problem when it comes to security-related code. Considering its effect on 
accountability and responsibility, evaluate the negative impact of this 
development and propose a strategy to mitigate this behavior. Briefly explain 
how your strategy addresses these concerns. (5 points)

Drawing on your knowledge from the lecture, briefly explain what each of the

change the role of managers in organizations. Weigh the potential advantages

Executive Summary
IS project managers regularly face the issue of whether to use temporary external 
personnel to augment internal personnel on software development projects. Based on 
interviews within 16 organizations, we found that viewing the use of external hires 
simply as a stop-gap measure can mask potential long-term impacts on an organization’s 
capabilities to undertake current and future software development initiatives. Our 
findings indicate that the implications of using temporary external personnel go beyond 
the immediate objective of addressing skill shortages and cover a variety of increasingly 
important issues, specifically: 
•	
Developing internal staff skill-sets and organizational software development 
capabilities
•	
Capturing, storing, accessing, and disseminating knowledge gained from external 
hires
•	
Planning for current and future software development projects. 
We present our findings on the challenges associated with this sourcing alternative and 
provide solutions that organizations have used to address their long-term IS human 
resource needs.
USING TEMPORARY EXTERNAL PROJECT 
PERSONNEL HAS WIDER IMPLICATIONS
Internal project teams often have to be augmented by temporary external personnel 
because project-related skills and/or manpower are not available in-house. While 
the scope of such personnel sourcing decisions may appear to be limited to specific 
projects, the collective impact of a series of such decisions can have far-reaching 
effects on the capabilities and performance of an organization’s software development 
group. The often-expressed attitude of many organizations is: “If we don’t have it, and 
it’s available, we just go out and get it.”2 
We argue that it is important to consider the reasons for a given personnel shortage 
when deciding on the best sourcing option. In addition, there is a second—and more 
critical—issue associated with using external personnel: What happens after the 
project is finished and an external contractor leaves? If this issue is not effectively 
addressed, its ramifications can affect not only the particular project but future 
software development initiatives as well.
Decisions on whether to hire temporary external project personnel have much in 
common with deciding whether to outsource a specific project to a third party or 
carry it out internally. Two overriding themes emerge. First, organizations tend to 
in-source projects that are competitively important—that is, projects that provide 
technical or business capabilities perceived as important, near-term or far-term, in

distinguishing the organization from its competitors; 
outsourced projects tend to provide technical or 
business capabilities that are generally available from 
the marketplace.3 Second, when software development 
projects are outsourced, the arrangement with the 
external provider must be actively governed, mostly 
through the use of formal contracts.4 Governance 
issues are especially important given the potential for 
system development quality deficiencies to arise. Such 
deficiencies can result in unexpected costs that, in 
some cases, have been greater than the forecast total 
cost of carrying out a project in-house.5 
The decision to hire temporary external project 
personnel 
presents 
similar 
strategic 
concerns 
and governance challenges. From a governance 
perspective, project managers not only benefit from 
the use of formal contracts but also direct and control 
external personnel by integrating them into established 
project control structures. Strategically, a primary 
motive in deciding to augment in-house project 
personnel with external personnel is the flexibility 
that the software development group gains. Simply 
put, the software development group does not have to 
maintain as broad or as deep skill-sets that otherwise 
would be required to meet the requirements of its 
ongoing project portfolio.6 
However, hiring external personnel has significant 
implications for building and maintaining a software 
development group’s capabilities for current and 
future projects. One critical issue is the desirability of 
protecting and retaining an external hire’s knowledge, 
whether existing or created by carrying out his/her 
project role. The challenge of capturing knowledge 
stems from the need to retain both explicit and tacit 
knowledge. Explicit knowledge can be written down 
in a systematic manner; once captured, it is relatively 
easy to store and share. Tacit knowledge, on the other

A second critical issue is that the extensive use of 
temporary external personnel would seem to best align 
with the “task-focused” human resource mindset, 
where workers are seen as short-term producers. 
In contrast, the “human capital” mindset perceives

Unlike the task-focused mindset, the human capital

skills and capability of internal personnel (via, for 
example, training programs9 and knowledge-transfer10 
programs). 
Our research investigated the issues arising from 
augmenting in-house project staff with temporary 
external personnel. Based on interviews with 19 
individuals from 16 organizations (see the Appendix 
for more details), we present the findings from 
our research under five headings: filling expertise 
gaps and shortages, gaining or building software 
development capabilities, ramp-up issues with time-
compressed projects, retaining the knowledge held 
and created by temporary external hires, and the use of 
formal contracts.
FILLING EXPERTISE GAPS AND 
SHORTAGES
The decision to externally source some of a project 
team’s members invariably arises because of two 
types of expertise shortages: when the needed skill 
does not exist in the organization and when the needed 
skill does exist but is unavailable for a given project.

gaps) was largely caused by the constantly evolving

nature of information technologies deployed within 
the studied firms. There were two specific types of 
gaps: intentional and unintentional. 
Intentional expertise gaps occur when specific skill-
sets are viewed as being both not critical to a firm’s 
long-term viability and readily available, when 
needed, via the external market: 
“I don’t have a budget to get everyone I want, 
so I don’t fill needs I feel are not truly necessary 
for us. I look at three things before making this 
decision: is it central to our organization to 
have this skill, can we get it easily from the 
outside, and does it make sense from a cost 
perspective? We [employ] core [skills] but 
have had to outsource [to get] certain IT skills 
that aren’t core or necessary to our business.” 
(Firm J)11 
In contrast, unintentional expertise gaps arise 
from sudden personnel loss (e.g., retirements, job 
eliminations) and from evolving technology-induced 
market conditions. The latter lead to difficulties in 
hiring certain skills (e.g., when new skills surface or 
for knowledge domains whose strategic value has yet 
to be determined):
“There is always the possibility of some new 
technology coming out … In these situations, 
there is the potential of missing skill-sets 
[knowledge]. As technology changes occur, it 
can be a challenge to figure out what we really 
need for future development.” (Firm E)
As the nature of the technologies deployed by 
a firm evolves, the need for new IT-related core 
competencies emerges, and software development 
managers may suddenly find they have an expertise 
gap for a series of newly funded projects. During 
the 1990s, there were vivid examples of such 
unplanned expertise gaps in the areas of middleware, 
e-commerce, and ERP technologies, followed by 
shortages of COBOL programmers for Y2K projects. 
Finally, an organization may have people with the 
expertise needed for a new project, but they are 
currently deployed on other projects—ideally with 
higher or equal priority: 
“ … I have [many] people stretched to the 
limit, working on multiple projects. If I add just 
one more project to some [of their] workloads,

information about the size and industry of the firms in this study.
I may break them, so I may need to go out and 
get some help, even though we have the ability 
in-house. We do this sometimes to just tide 
things over, until resources become freed up.” 
(Firm B)
“I generally have fairly important projects, so 
I can … get whoever I need reassigned to me. 
When other issues trump this, then I will hire 
someone from the outside …” (Firm K)
Any of these skills gaps could fall into the intentional 
or unintentional categories. However, most of the 
interviewees in our study suggested that limited IS 
budgets and ongoing pressures to do more with less 
meant that using temporary external personnel to fill 
expertise gaps had become an essential part of today’s 
project management landscape.
GAINING OR BUILDING 
SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT 
CAPABILITIES
An unintentional expertise gap can be addressed by 
using an on-going project as a training platform, 
with external hires playing an important training 
role. While our interviewees mentioned a range of 
training-related outcomes, the two most common 
were building internal capabilities both for flexibility/
redundancy purposes and for supporting a project’s 
deployed technologies: 
“We have mentoring-type situations, where 
you can get placed on projects to learn as a 
type of ‘apprentice’—where you are really 
just an observer or might even help out a bit.” 
(Firm D)
“I use projects to train if possible … the main 
reason [being] supportability. You don’t want 
someone coming in and putting up a system 
and then walking out; then you can’t support 
it, you can’t maintain it.” (Firm C)
However, these training benefits have a cost—
typically, associated with the extra time and effort 
expended by key project personnel in mentoring, 
instructing, and repeating completed tasks for 
emphasis. Moreover, the extra time and effort 
expended by the project manager is often overlooked: 
“I usually spend more time on training projects 
[than I do on] a similar non-training project … 
With a typical project, I can assign a task and 
let the individual get on with it; I don’t have to 
look at their process too much, as long as they 
16    MIS Quarterly Executive Vol. 9 No. 1 / Mar 2010
© 2010 University of Minnesota
Wu and Zmud / Facing the Challenges of Temporary External IS Project Personnel
deliver. But with a training project I generally 
have to monitor the ‘training process’ to make 
sure what needs to get passed along is done 
in-process.”(Firm H)
“The extra time I need to devote to a training 
project comes from my need to check the 
training process constantly: is the information 
getting passed to the trainee, is the trainee 
getting and assimilating the information? … 
if not, I or the trainee will ask the external 
worker to stop and go back some steps in the 
process.” (Firm L)
RAMP-UP ISSUES WITH TIME-
COMPRESSED PROJECTS 
Two ramp-up issues surfaced when interviewees 
were asked about the viability of using external 
personnel for time-compressed projects or projects 
with shortened deadlines. The first issue concerns the 
use of external project personnel versus inexperienced 
internal staff. There was general agreement that tight 
deadlines made it difficult to train internal personnel 
in new skill-sets and that deploying external personnel 
was the more viable tactic when experienced internal 
staff were unavailable:
“I’d rather use outside experts, as they have 
already utilized the skill effectively in different 
settings. Especially, with a need to deliver 
quickly ... If I had all the time I needed, having 
my staff learn on the project would be great, 
but probably… not very timely.” (Firm L)
The second concerns the difficulty of using external 
personnel when a time-compressed project requires 
deep knowledge of internal systems and processes: 
“The project was all internally driven due to 
time constraints and the fact that we needed 
people to know our systems. We didn’t have 
time to get outside developers up to speed on 
our systems.” (Firm B)
There was a consensus view on the best tactic to 
follow when an external hire would need to develop 
a rich understanding of organizational-specific issues 
before he or she can work on a time-compressed 
project. In this situation, it is better to reassign a 
qualified internal staff member from another (not 
time-compressed) project to that project and to assign 
the external hire to the other project.
RETAINING THE KNOWLEDGE 
HELD AND CREATED BY 
TEMPORARY EXTERNAL HIRES 
All interviewees in our study stressed the need to 
actively manage the knowledge-retention processes 
associated with the use of temporary external 
personnel. They described variations of three 
distinct methods of knowledge capture: mandated 
documentation, using technical writers to produce 
documentation, and shadowing. Table 1 summarizes 
the number of firms employing each of these methods. 
MANDATED DOCUMENTATION
Nine out of the 14 firms that used mandated 
documentation from external personnel included this 
requirement in the contract: 
“We ask all external hires to write up a report 
detailing what they did before leaving. It 
is part of the contract we have with them.”
(Firm J)
In the other five firms, the requirement to prepare 
knowledge documentation was a personal obligation 
placed on external hires by the project managers we 
interviewed. The level of documentation involved 
could vary from a final written report by the external 
hire before departing to daily activity reports: 
“I ask them to document everything they do on 
a daily basis. If you wait, things can slip, so I 
want them to write it down as soon as possible 
…” (Firm N)
Three of our interviewees stated that in addition to 
requiring external hires to document their activities, 
they were also required to provide an “exit briefing” 
attended by all project team members. Verification of 
the documentation created by external hires could be 
carried out at these Q&A briefings. The briefings also 
helped begin the knowledge-integration process as 
internal team members could raise questions related
