Administration, and an organization-wide project 
manager pool was set up.
1.2. Foster the Assertiveness of Steering 
Committees and Project Sponsors. The Swiss 
Federal Administration established clear rules for 
decision-making at the project governance level. 
For instance, steering committees now include at 
least one representative of each affected business 
and IT unit, with decision-making power and 
influence lying within the line organization.
1.3. Pay Attention to the Line Organization’s 
Budgeting 
Cycles 
and 
Procurement 
Procedures. In the projects we analyzed, not 
only did the line organization’s budgeting cycle 
(e.g., one fiscal year) need to be considered 
in a project’s financials and schedules, but 
also complex procedures dictated by public 
procurement law. The HERMES standard has 
been amended to include approval of the plan 
components as a defined responsibility of the 
steering committee at the end of the initiation 
phase. These approvals take account of the 
budgeting cycles and procurement procedures. 
 2. Triage Recommendations: Prevent a 
Mission Impossible
Because even excellent project management 
cannot save a project situated within an adverse 
context, we provide three recommendations for 
triaging projects with the aim of preventing a 
mission impossible. 
2.1. Only Start or Continue a Project 
if Context-Related Risks Are Known and 
Manageable. A rule was added to HERMES that 
forces steering committees to assess a project’s 
context in the initiation phase so that they can 
make informed “go/no-go” decisions. Moreover, 
steering committees now need to define criteria 
for subsequent phase approvals, taking account 
not only of the deliverables and other project 
management-related factors but also the five 
contextual factors. As a part of a project’s risk 
assessment, at least one assessment is now 
required by an internal or external expert who 
is independent of project management. The 
questions listed in Table 2 are used as the basis 
for assessing the context.
2.2. Prevent Over-Optimism at the Project 
Governance Level. The Federal IT Steering Unit 
has now established a strong but nonbinding 
recommendation (and reference guideline) to 
assign independent, neutral (active or retired) 
senior managers as “sparring partners” to the 
project sponsor and steering committee of a large 
IT-related project. The role of these independent 
managers is to prevent overoptimism at the 
project governance level.
2.3. 
Minimize 
the 
Technological 
and 
Organizational Complexity of Projects. This 
recommendation encourages the implementation 
of smaller projects instead of bundling as many 
deliverables as possible into one massive and 
unwieldy project covering all technological and 
organizational areas. Executives of the federal 
offices are encouraged by the Federal IT Steering 
Unit to modularize big endeavors so that the 
resulting projects can be handled in a more agile 
way. Modularization allows project management 
to address both technological and organizational 
complexity by reducing interdependencies and 
avoiding being “left in the dark” for too long. This 
recommendation was formalized by amending 
the HERMES project standard to include a 
hybrid method for guiding projects comprising 
traditional as well as agile elements.
3. Ability Recommendations: Establish 
and Improve Project Governance Skills
These three recommendations address the 
general lack of capability or ignorance at the 
project governance level to handle contextual 
factors properly.
3.1. 
Define 
and 
Communicate 
Tasks, 
Competences and Responsibilities for Project 
Sponsors 
and 
Steering 
Committees. 
The 
Federal IT Steering Unit introduced a short 
manual that guides project sponsors and steering 
committees in defining their tasks, competencies 
and responsibilities during a project lifecycle. 
As 
well 
as 
specifying 
project 
governance 
roles, the manual guides steering committee 
meetings through standard agenda items and 
defines compulsory project checkpoints. It is 
kept as short as possible as executives in charge 
demanded 
straightforward 
guidance. 
The 
majority of steering committees and project 
sponsors of projects within the Federal IT 
Steering Unit now work in accordance with this 
manual.
3.2. Provide Professional Development for 
Executives Who Are (or Will Be) Performing 
Project Governance Roles. The Federal IT

Steering Unit was convinced that “classic” 
professional development provided via training 
or courses was not suitable for the target group. 
Instead, it addresses the need for the professional 
development 
of 
executives 
in 
a 
project 
governance function through a community of 
practice within the Swiss Federal Administration 
established for that purpose. The Federal IT 
Steering Unit also encourages active participation 
in a community of practice that brings together 
executives 
from 
various 
organizations 
to 
discuss project governance issues with steering 
committee members, project managers and 
project portfolio managers from other projects or 
programs. 
3.3. 
Establish 
Independent 
Project 
Governance Quality Control. The Federal IT 
Steering Unit has extended its standard project 
auditing procedure (which is focused at the 
project management level and is conducted by 
the Swiss Federal Audit Office for the attention 
of the Federal Council) to include a review of 
each project’s governance performance. Every 
IT-related project within the Swiss Federal 
Administration that is defined as an “ICT key 
project” is subject to such an audit.26 The audit 
provides “praise and blame” for project sponsors 
and steering committees, and makes suggestions 
for improvement. Audit findings and suggestions 
are reinforced by the external sparring partners 
who not only help to prevent overoptimism 
and foster good faith, but also act as coaches to 
improve project governance skills and the context 
awareness of project sponsors and steering 
committees.
4. Collaboration Recommendations: 
Ensure Effective Collaboration 
Between the Project Sponsor/Steering 
Committee and Project Manager
Our research shows that well-functioning, 
professional interplay at the project governance 
and project management levels is a prerequisite 
for project success. This is especially important 
for dealing with a project’s contextual factors, 
where a lack of effective opportunities for 
discourse at the project management and project 
governance levels inhibits effective collaboration.

Organizations should not see the increased 
overhead resulting from enhanced collaboration 
as a burden but as an investment in reducing the 
risk of failure. We provide two recommendations 
for ensuring effective collaboration. 
4.1. Ensure Effective Discourse Between 
Project Governance and Project Management 
Personnel 
on 
the 
Project’s 
Continually 
Changing Context. The Federal IT Steering Unit 
implemented this recommendation by including 
defined exchange platforms and specific topics 
for discussion by project management and project 
governance personnel in the HERMES standard. 
HERMES now requires regular meetings (e.g., 
at least every four weeks) between project 
management and the steering committee and also 
defines the topics that need to be discussed (risks, 
budget, time, scope and contextual factors) as 
well as communication principles (e.g., reporting 
honestly, refraining from glossing over problems 
and taking each other seriously). 
4.2. Create Common Ground at the Project 
Governance and Project Management Levels at 
the Beginning of the Project. From the projects 
we examined, it was clear that providing the 
project management team with a written project 
mission statement and/or project charter was not 
sufficient for creating common ground between 
the project management team and steering 
committee members. To address this problem, 
the Federal IT Steering Unit has tested a new 
tool (called “project canvas session”27), which is 
being considered for inclusion in the HERMES 
project standard. This tool will ensure that, at the 
outset of a new project, the project management 
team, the project sponsor and steering committee 
members engage in a discussion, supported by 
visual aids, to create common understanding of 
the project’s context and management.
Concluding Comments
For complex, large IT projects, state-of-the-
art project management is a necessary but not 
sufficient condition for success. In the four 
“well-managed but failed” projects we analyzed, 
project governance bodies launched projects 
with missions that were impossible to accomplish 
because the steering committees overlooked or

did not adequately address various contextual 
challenges. In some of the cases, contextual 
challenges were not addressed from the start of 
the project; in others, they were not addressed 
as the project progressed. Illustrated by evidence 
from these four projects, we have presented a 
framework for analyzing a project’s contextual 
factors and provided recommendations that will 
enable steering committees to avoid missions 
impossible and keep large, complex projects on 
track.
We 
believe 
that 
our 
findings 
and 
recommendations 
will

Executive Summary1,2
In this article, we identify extensions to traditional project management methods that have 
been successfully used for large, radically innovative IT projects—projects that include 
points that deviate significantly from those encountered in previous projects. We term 
these as “innovation points.” We found that project managers from eight different firms 
who had each managed such a project had independently converged on a common set of 
solutions to problems that occur in managing innovation points, solutions that are not 
addressed by traditional project management practices. In each of the eight cases, highly 
regarded IT project managers applied the traditional, managed life-cycle, stage-gate 
approach embodied in the Project Management Institute’s methodologies. In each case, 
these presumed best practices were found to be inadequate and were extended to create 
a new dual-process approach. After describing this dual-process approach and providing 
additional field evidence that it can be widely applied to large, complex IT projects, we 
provide guidelines for adopting it. 
EXTENDING TRADITIONAL PROJECT MANAGEMENT 
PRACTICES TO HANDLE INNOVATION POINTS
Recent re-examinations of the Manhattan project3 and the Polaris Missile project4 
have raised questions about the effectiveness of current project management practices 
used for large IT projects, especially for those that contain a great deal of uncertainty. 
Although these classic projects spawned nearly all modern-day project management 
methodologies,5 these re-examinations suggest that modern-day methodologies 
would have been completely ineffective for managing these seminal projects because 
they fail to take non-trivial innovation into account and focus entirely on a control-
centric, “stage-gate” approach.6 To be effective, today’s project management methods 
need be extended to include techniques that recognize and manage uncertainty and 
innovation.7
IT projects are inherently high-risk endeavors under the best of conditions. In the 
2009 Standish report of IT project failures, only 32% of projects were deemed to have 
been successful.8 Although many of the reasons cited for project failure are outside the 
control of IT project managers, these managers do control the project methods they 
use.

PURPOSE OF THIS STUDY AND 
RESEARCH APPROACH 
This article reports on our research to better define the 
methods used by PMI-certified9 project managers to 
successfully manage relatively large IT development 
efforts that are highly innovative in nature. Our 
findings are based on what we learned from PMI-
certified project managers in eight firms (referred 
to anonymously in this article) who described the 
practices they developed for IT projects that share 
three characteristics: 
1.	 The project included multiple “innovation 
points”10 with radically innovative issues 
(which we refer to as “radical innovation 
points”11)
2.	 The project size was perceived to be large
3.	 Current PMI methods were found to be 
completely inadequate for the project. 
These eight highly innovative IT projects were highly 
diverse and included, for example, the development of 
an online textbook delivery system (involving three 
different publishing firms with over 50 combined 
developers), a video-on-demand delivery system, and 
a credit card processing system for use at individual 
gas pumps. 
All eight of the projects were considered to be large-
size efforts by their respective project managers. 
9  The Project Management Institute (PMI) is a globally recognized 
organization that had certified over 390,000 project management 
professionals as of 2010.
10  The term “innovation point” refers to a portion of an IT project 
that is (1) conceptually cohesive (e.g., a task on a Pert chart) and (2) 
requires some non-trivial decision making (e.g., innovation of some 
sort even if it is only incremental in nature). We coined this term based 
on the terminology used by the project managers we interviewed for 
this study. They used terms such as “innovative,” “new components,” 
“areas of innovation,” “discovery pages,” and “new design segments” 
to refer to parts of their projects they deemed to be innovative design 
issues. Project management planning convention, as per the best 
practices codified by the PMI in its guide Project Management Book of 
Knowledge Guide (Project Management Institute, 2011), is to plan and 
execute projects by breaking them down into workable sections. In this 
article, we refer to these project sections as innovation points, which 
can be conventional or radical.  
11  The large body of literature about Radical Innovation is most 
often attributed to the seminal work of Zaltman, G., Duncan, R., and 
Holbek, J. Innovations and Organizations, John Wiley and Sons, 
1973. Radical Innovation in IT projects is described in papers such 
as Carlo, J., Lyytinen, K., and Rose, G. “Internet Computing As a 
Disruptive Information Technology Innovation: The Role of Strong 
Order Effects,” Information Systems Journal (21:1), January 2011, pp. 
91-122. For clarity, we use the term “Radical Innovation Points” where 
project attributes match the “Uncertain,” “Incremental Innovation,” or 
“Conventional” project attributes that would be “Moderately Novel” as 
described in Lenfle, S., and Loch, C., op. cit., 2010.
 
However, as shown by the following quotes, the 
project managers’ conception of “large-size” projects 
with a significant number of radical innovation points 
varied considerably:
“Large to me means something that utilizes 
15+ individuals … also we are talking about 
something that can take a sizeable amount of 
time … 9+ months to over 2 years.” (Project 
Manager, Firm 1)
“Large typically involves people from outside 
the U.S.—places like Brazil and Europe. There 
is typically a central core group in the U.S., 
with 10-15 people, and people in these groups 
will manage another set of 10-15 at these 
other locations. So … 100-150-plus.” (Project 
Manager, Firm 3)
“Large projects tend to take more than a year 
for us and will typically entail using people 
across multiple departments, not just IT. We 
have had anywhere from 20 to 40-plus people 
on these types of projects.” (Project Manager, 
Firm 7)
These comments are consistent with software engineer 
Larry Constantine’s definition of large IT projects: 
“Size is in the eye of the beholder … for 
example, some organizations may consider a 
20-person project to be huge whereas others 
may consider a 200-person project to be 
merely mid-size.”12
Each of the eight project managers had independently 
invented a new approach that they attributed the 
success of their projects to. Based on our analysis 
of these extensions to existing PMI guidelines, we 
describe a new, dual-methodology approach for 
large, non-conventional IT projects that had, in 
effect, been created by these project managers. We 
then subsequently validated these ideas with 25 other 
PMI-certified project managers in 22 firms of varying 
size. The net result is a set of recommendations for 
extending current standard project management 
methodologies to manage radical innovation points 
in large IT projects and thus increase the likelihood 
of project success. (Full details of the research 
methodology can be found in the Appendix.)

Recognizing and Managing Innovation Points in Large IT Projects
TRADITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF 
LARGE IT PROJECTS
Current PMI project management methods used for IT 
projects are based on a life-cycle or phased stage-gate 
approach and assume the system requirements have 
been clearly defined at the start of a project. The PMI 
has focused on codifying and espousing best practice 
techniques in methodologies aimed at governance and 
control. This methodical approach makes sense and 
brings a needed sense of order to the management of 
IT projects, especially those that have very clearly 
defined paths and well-understood project goals.13 
Much of the research into IT project management 
retrospectively examines large-scale projects, in 
particular large project failures.14 Such studies focus 
on conventional project management processes and 
methodologies. Even research frameworks created to 
raise project managers’ awareness of typical IT project 
risks are primarily focused on a well-known set of 
problems within projects.15 
Some researchers’ response to managing increased 
complexity and uncertainty in large IT efforts has 
been to advocate stronger controls.16 However, these 
researchers have admitted that stronger controls do 
not remove all these inherent difficulties: “Stronger 
controls by themselves cannot lead to project 
success.”17 Others have noted that “The discipline of 
project management should be broadened in order 
to create greater value for organizations whose 
portfolios include novel and uncertain projects.”18 Our 
study reported in this article was aimed at contributing 
to a broadening of the project management discipline. 
We first describe the three categories of issues that 
arose as the eight project managers were managing 
what to them were radically innovative IT projects:

PRE-PLANNING TO IDENTIFY 
INNOVATION POINTS
There was a consensus among the eight project 
managers about the importance of identifying 
areas in the project that were considered highly 
unconventional in nature. Each of their projects 
contained an abundance of both incremental/
conventional and radical innovation points throughout 
their entire scope. But it was the radical innovation 
points that most preoccupied the project managers and 
were the cause of the greatest stress and risk: 
“We knew we couldn’t do what was typically 
done … so we spent a lot of upfront time 
to understand everything, or as much of 
everything, we could.” (Project Manager, Firm 
1) 
 “I started with so many questions regarding 
the project … much, much more than I would 
typically have. And I mean IT projects that I 
had completed ... that were similar in size [and 
time], would have their share of questions and 
issues during planning, but this thing was 
way beyond anything I had ever experienced 
… I had to deal with a number of issues and 
questions before we could even get moving.” 
(Project Manager, Firm 3)
The eight project managers clearly recognized 
their respective projects included major deviations 
from conventional projects and dealt with technical 
issues that could not be solved by well-understood 
technological means or incremental innovation: 
“We identified a number of challenges that 
we had no blueprints for tackling … no one 
had seen these problems before … we were 
treading new ground.” (Project Manager, Firm 
2)
All the project managers felt the initial time spent 
on identifying these radical innovation points had 
saved them considerable amounts of time during 
project planning and execution. One project manager 
illustrated the importance of identifying and pre-
planning for radical innovation points by describing

Overall, this approach allowed the project manager,

the radical innovation points into manageable sub-

be fairly lengthy. Yet, each project manager was clear 
the extra upfront time was more than offset by the 
benefits:
“Even though it sounds like a lot of time, 
when I look back now, it helped us plan for 
and anticipate a number of … problems. We 
could then break down a project based on the 
identified issues and have different groups start 
working on them … sometimes in tandem.” 
(Project Manager, Firm 2)
All eight project managers said that the projects they 
were describing were the most innovative they had 
ever managed. However, the projects still contained 
a mix of conventional and radical innovation points. 
Because of this, all eight stressed that they found 
great value in extending, not replacing, the traditional 
PMI guidelines.  The extensions were themselves 
radical process innovations19  taking the form of a 
novel, dual-methodology that manages both types of 
innovation points.
MANAGING INNOVATION POINTS
Each of the eight project managers reported that they 
handled the radical and conventional portions of their 
projects differently. At the highest level of abstraction, 
conventional innovation points were effectively 
managed through traditional best practices embedded 
in methodologies like those from the PMI. These 
methodologies are based on the standard IT project 
management life-cycle that can be found in typical IT 
project management texts (see Figure 1). Within this 
life-cycle, organizations will typically initiate projects 
that have been approved for development. Projects are 
then scoped and planned in accordance to the specified 
requirements. Execution of the plan with appropriate 
changes and adjustments to its scope occurs until 
the project reaches a final resolution (delivery or 
termination). The PMI recognizes that a series of 
key knowledge areas (time, cost, scope, risk, quality, 
communications, HR, procurement, and integration) 
must be managed within this framework.20

However, the project managers had to deviate from 
the standard project management guidelines to enable 
them to effectively manage the radical innovation 
points, which typically were accompanied by massive 
learning barriers that had to be overcome.22 The 
challenge facing these project managers was how to 
effectively deal with any radical innovation points 
identified. It was extremely important from a planning 
and execution perspective:
“You need to at least have some idea as to 
how to approach this type of project, so good 
upfront work is crucial. Especially when it 
comes to timing and planning out such a 
project.” (Project Manager, Firm 7) 
 “… thinking outside of the box was needed. 
We couldn’t take things on head-on, given the 
large number of technical issues presented 
by the project. We had to execute these parts 
differently” (Project Manager, Firm 5)
All eight project managers, independently of each 
other, had developed a distinct method to handle their 
radical innovation points. As noted above, the pre-
planning stage was common to all eight projects. The 
first pre-planning step was to identify and prioritize 
the radical innovation points: 
“With the technical issues we had never dealt 
with before, we chunked things down into more 
manageable pieces. I looked upon them as 
unique problems that we had to find solutions 
for.” (Project Manager, Firm 1)
 “The only thing that made sense was to go 
after the problem one piece at a time. It just 
made things more manageable … not so 
daunting a task.” (Project Manager, Firm 6)
Once identified, the second step was to treat the 
radical innovation points as unique sub-projects within 
the overall project and give them priority over all the 
other portions of the project. While an IT project is 
typically planned and executed in sequence, these 
projects began by executing the radical innovation 
point sub-projects as soon as possible. In each case, 
the project manager assigned dedicated personnel to 
explore potential solutions for the innovation points. 
The main reason given for adopting this approach was 
uncertainty about the time needed to resolve a radical 
innovation point:

The third deviation from the standard IT project 
process arose from a need to explore multiple 
solutions for the radical innovation points. Each one 
required a diversified problem-solving approach that 
involved exploring and evaluating parallel multiple 
potential solutions. A continuous cycle of exploration23 
and execution ruled out potential deadends until a 
viable solution was discovered. 
While segmentation in general appears consistent with 
traditional IT project planning (as would be seen in a 
work-breakdown schedule),24 there are three important 
differences in the approach adopted by the eight 
project managers. First, traditional planning does not 
identify sub-components of a project based on degree 
of innovation:
“We used this time to hash out the problems 
we knew would appear during the project. 
I’m talking about issues we hadn’t dealt 
with before, things really different and never 
encountered before by anyone but that we 
could anticipate given the unique nature of 
this project.” (Project Manager, Firm 8)
Second, traditional methods do not allow for 
significant time for exploring multiple solutions 
to fulfill the requirements for completing sub-
components: 
“Even though we spent what might seem a lot 
of upfront prep time, in our case five weeks, we 
needed it to start looking at the true scope of 
this project.” (Project Manager, Firm 7)

innovation points require a more malleable roadmap 
or set of roadmaps to be developed. Large portions 
of the eight highly innovative projects dealt with new 
or unexplored technologies, which meant multiple 
paths had to be explored to arrive at viable potential 
solutions. In the words of one of the project managers:
“We were constantly looking at different 
solutions all the time. We weren’t sure what 
would work, so multiple teams always worked 
towards a solution on a specific issue.” 
(Project Manager, Firm 6)
This exploration process went hand-in-hand with 
the execution of the project. As less promising paths 
were eliminated and more promising solutions were 
pursued, the other parts of the project (both related 
and unrelated) would be re-scoped and re-planned as 
necessary, which led to a constantly evolving scope-
execution-exploration change cycle. 
“We needed to communicate constantly and 
make sure everyone was on the same page. 
Once a potential solution [was] decided upon, 
it could impact others on the project … so we 
made sure everyone was in the loop. And this 
was a constant process that never ended—
well not until the project was done.” (Project 
Manager, Firm 7)
In some cases, the need to adjust could mean 
discarding any and all project planning that had been 
prepared for after the radical innovation point:
“If we chose path C to solve one problem, but 
it caused problems with some other parts of the 
project down the line, we may have to go back 
and say … let’s use path B, even though path C 
might be the optimal solution on a stand-alone 
basis. Path B was the optimal project solution 
since it would allow us to move other parts 
[innovation-points] of the project along.” 
(Project Manager, Firm 6)
Adapting to changes constantly and appropriately was 
paramount for continual progression through the eight 
highly innovative projects. In one firm, the solutions 
to radical innovation points (referred to as “discovery 
pages”) were examined and ranked for their viability 
in achieving the desired technical outcome before 
attempting to integrate them with the core IT project: 
 “… we [created] discovery pages which were 
rapid durations through technical issues. 
We tested as much as possible, for potential 
problems in the project, before integrating 
them into the actual project.” (Project 
Manager, Firm 8) 
In this firm, there was an iterative cycle of 
exploration, which took place immediately after the 
radical innovation points (discovery pages) had been 
identified and ranked. The cycle comprised a series 
of mini-technical projects to resolve these points, 
followed by integration with the core project. This 
cycle continued until the main project was completed 
or terminated. Because these mini-projects required 
multiple exploratory paths, the ability and willingness 
to explore, along with the ability to adapt rapidly, 
were essential for the success of the overall project.
As another project manager stated: 
“A radical or high-innovation project is 
basically a series of discoveries that are 
required to complete the whole.” (Project 
Manager, Firm 1)
From our discussions with the eight project managers, 
it is clear that they all adjusted the traditional project 
life-cycle to identify and handle issues relating to 
radical innovation points. We have synthesized the 
approaches into the dual project management life-
cycle approach depicted in Figure 2. 
This revision to the traditional project life-cycle 
includes a pre-planning process for identifying, 
ranking, and prioritizing radical innovation points. 
Following identification and prioritization, exploration 
for potential solutions is initiated, while a malleable 
plan for the overall project is created. Overall project 
planning should be fairly flexible (and in some 
cases, incomplete), because the plan may need to be 
adjusted in response to the solutions found for the 
radical innovation points. The conventional portions 
of the project still follow the traditional planning, 
execution, and change management process, but 
the execution of these parts occurs in parallel with 
exploration of solutions for the radical innovation 
points. As innovation point solutions are found, both 
the execution and the planning of the project may 
have to be adjusted. This iterative cycle of planning, 
execution in parallel with exploration, and re-planning 
occurs until all the innovation points within the project 
have been dealt with. 
PROJECT MANAGER SKILLS
The frequent changes to project plans and execution 
resulting from the multiple radical innovation points 
encountered in the eight projects required project 
managers to adapt quickly and adjust the project plan 
appropriately. Once a solution to a radical innovation 
point had been settled on, the project manager needed 
to ascertain what impact this solution would have on

CONFIRMATION THAT THE 
DUAL-LEVEL PROCESS CAN BE 
WIDELY APPLIED 
In the dual-level process for planning and executing 
radical IT projects described above, the eight project 
managers had extended their organizations’ standard 
IT project processes for conventional portions within 
their projects to also handle radical innovation points 
(as shown in Figure 2). We believe this integrated 
project management approach can be applied to 
other large IT projects that require some degree of 
innovation. We tested this hypothesis with a wider 
group of project management professionals, to 
confirm its viability in practice. 
Between December 2010 and May 2011, we 
conducted follow-up interviews with 25 additional 
project managers. Their responses clearly indicated 
they could see the benefit of applying the dual-
level process for large and complex IT projects. 
In particular, they thought the idea of identifying 
potential radical innovation points before the project 
was planned was a viable addition to current project 
management processes. All 25 recalled managing at 
least one large and complex IT project that included 
more than one radical innovation point. These 
innovation points had not been identified in advance, 
which resulted in significant and very costly delays. 
Each of these project managers also could see the 
merit of having a preliminary period during which 
radical innovation points are identified, especially 
for large IT efforts. Likewise, 17 of the 25 saw the 
value of isolating a radical innovation point into a 
sub-project to be worked on as soon as possible for 
development and eventual integration back into the 
main project. A few project managers even reflected 
on previous large efforts and speculated:
“I wish we had done this on the … project I 
was on. I can just imagine the pitfalls and time 
we could have saved.” 
 “… on one particular portion of our … project, 
we probably wasted three to four months going 
around in circles. I can see how this may have 
really saved us at least three weeks of time … 
maybe more.” 
All 25 concluded that the conventional aspects of 
their projects could be managed with current project 
management approaches, while the radical innovation 
point portions had to be addressed in a manner akin to 
the techniques presented in this study. 
GUIDELINES FOR MANAGING 
LARGE IT PROJECTS
We provide five guidelines for using the techniques 
identified by our study for managing large IT projects 
that include radical innovation. 
Guideline 1: Assign Project Managers 
Who Can Cope with Both Conventional 
and Radical Innovation Points in Large 
IT Projects
IT executives and managers should recognize that 
large IT projects will likely include both conventional 
development points and radical innovation points, 
and that a blend of new and traditional project 
management techniques will be required. The dual 
project management life-cycle process is not an 
entirely new methodology but instead incorporates 
both traditional and new aspects. 
Further, this dual-process requires project managers 
who have the skills to effectively cope both with 
conventional points and with radical innovation points 
in the same project. As shown in this study, three of 
the eight highly innovative projects required a change 
of project manager in mid-stream; though highly 
skilled project managers were initially assigned to 
these three projects, they were not able to cope with 
the multiple, radical innovation points.

Guideline 2: Recognize the Need to 
Identify Radical Innovation Points at the 
Pre-planning Stage
In all of the eight successful radical innovation IT 
projects that are the focus of this study, the project 
managers allocated upfront time, prior to any project 
planning, to identify their projects’ radical innovation 
points. Having identified these points, they then 
brought together key individuals to identify and 
brainstorm solutions to them. Allowing time for these 
activities prior to project planning and execution 
serves two key purposes. First, it identifies foreseeable 
radical innovation points within the project. Second, it 
allows the project manager time to properly plan for 
handling the points and integrating their solutions into 
the overall framework of the project. 
Guideline 3: Use Multiple Teams 
with Diverse Knowledge to Develop 
Solutions for the Radical Innovation 
Points
Project managers must identify the appropriate 
resources (personnel, technology, etc.) required to 
solve the radical innovation points that have been 
identified and explore potential avenues for addressing 
them. By dividing up resources into smaller, more 
focused teams with diverse knowledge, resources 
can be more effectively directed toward developing 
appropriate and successful solutions for radical 
innovation points. 
Guideline 4: Choose Radical Innovation 
Point Solutions that are Best for the 
Overall Project 
Radical innovation point solutions may have potential 
ramifications throughout the entire project because 
they may involve new technologies, platforms, and 
development techniques. As such, they can potentially 
impact not only future steps within the project but also 
steps already completed. While a newly discovered 
radical innovation point solution could be the most 
effective or most efficient solution to the problem at 
hand, it could potentially be non-viable in the context 
of the whole project. When deciding which radical 
innovation point solution to adopt, it is important 
to take a holistic approach and assess whether the 
optimum solution for just a portion of the project is 
the one that is best for the entire project.
Guideline 5: Be Flexible and Adaptable 
When Implementing Radical Innovation 
Point Solutions 
To effectively integrate radical innovation point 
solutions requires a flexible mindset throughout the 
duration of the project. The project manager and those 
working on the project must be able to quickly adjust 
to new options, and project plans must be flexible so 
that they can be adapted to changing innovation point 
solutions.
CONCLUDING COMMENTS
Recent retrospective reviews of managing highly 
innovative, large-scale development efforts have 
identified the need to develop project management 
methods that go beyond traditional practices. In this 
study, we have identified the processes used in eight 
highly innovative, relatively large IT projects that 
were successful and have synthesized our findings 
to create a dual project management life-cycle 
process for managing these types of IT development 
efforts. We believe it is important for IT executives 
to 
recognize 
the 
importance 
of 
dual-process 
methodological approaches. Although we would 
caution against applying our findings to all “large” 
IT projects—since different project managers in our 
study perceived “large” in different ways—we have 
used the insights and validations gained from our field 
interviews to propose a series of guidelines to help 
project management professionals more effectively 
manage innovative IT projects with high levels of 
uncertainty. Whether an IT project contains one or 
many radical innovation points, we believe the ability 
to identify, effectively resolve, and integrate these 
components into the overall project is crucial for IT 
project success. 
APPENDIX: RESEARCH METHOD
Given the qualitative nature of this study, we 
conducted a multi-site, theory-building case study 
across 29 Fortune 500 firms.25 The research design 
was aimed at generating and testing theoretical 
insights gleaned across the multiple sites.26 To increase

We conducted a series of on-site and telephone 
interviews between April 2008 and June 2009 with 39 
experienced IT professionals from the 29 firms, who 
were involved with numerous IT development efforts 
as project managers. All 39 semi-structured interviews 
were tape-recorded, generating 65 hours of voice-
recorded material. Transcriptions of the recordings 
created over 800 pages of text. 
All the participants were members of the Project 
Management Institute, with 33 being PMI-certified 
project managers and the rest in the process of gaining 
certification. The initial interviews lasted from 45 to 
70 minutes with questions posed to identify project 
managers who had managed at least one radically 
innovative, large IT project.
Using Peters’ definition of radical innovation as the 
basis for defining highly innovative IT projects,28 each 
of the project managers was asked to describe the 
most innovative IT project they had managed. They 
were then asked to rate the project they had described 
on a scale of 1 to 5 (1=no innovation involved in the 
project, 2=some minor innovative issues, 3=project 
was equally balanced between innovative and known 
IT project issues, 4=project was predominantly 
innovative in nature, with over half of the issues 
on the project being innovative or radical in nature, 
5=project was completely innovative in nature, never 
attempted before).

their projects as being radically innovative (i.e., 
rated as 4 or 5), representing eight firms in different

Introduction
This document helps you with formatting your case study report. It
is both a template and a manual. To write your report, replace the
content of the manual with the content of your report and save your
report in a separate Word file. Please note: This template was
created on Windows 10 using Microsoft Word version 2210. The
names of menu items and buttons may vary from version to version.
Additionally, some terms such as the name of styles and menu
buttons depend on the language you have set in your Microsoft
Office package. When using this template, we recommend setting
the language to English. To do so, click on the File tab in the upper
left corner. Click on “Options” at the bottom of the sidebar on the
left and then on “Language”. Here you can define English as your
preferred language. Please note that this template is based on our
chair’s thesis template which is why certain aspects may not be
relevant to your report.
Using the Template
Text Formatting
All text in your report should be formatted with a style. The styles
can be found in the Home tab in the section Styles. For the main
text, use the “Normal” style. Unless you select a different style,
Word formats the text according to this style. To highlight text, you
can format it strong, italic or underlined. This is possible using the
buttons in the Home tab in the Font section or using the
correspondingly named styles.
Besides changing the font, you can also use lists to make your text
easier to apprehend. Two different list types are available for this
purpose:
Unnumbered List
Numbered List
You can add unnumbered lists by clicking the “Bullets” button in
the Home tab, in the section Paragraph. Alternatively, after clicking
the “Multilevel List” button, you can select the "Unnumbered List"
list style. There or by means of the tab key you can change the list
level to create a structured list. Please do not change the preset
bullets.
To add a numbered list, click on the “Numbering” button in the
section Paragraph of the Home tab or select the “Numbered List”
template after clicking on the “Multilevel List” button. Changing the
list levels is done analogously to unnumbered lists.
Structure
Use headings to structure your work and format the headings using
the appropriate styles. You can use styles for headings at three
levels. Do not use deeper levels. By using the appropriate styles,
headings automatically appear in the table of content. If you want
to structure a paragraph below the third level, you can insert a
subheading and format it using the style Subheading.
Visualizations
Tables
The comprehensibility of scientific papers usually benefits from
visualizing content with tables and figures. To insert a table, click
the “Table” button in the Insert tab and select the desired number
of rows and columns. Alternatively, you can import tables from
other software applications, such as Microsoft Excel. You can adjust
the number of rows and columns as well as their width and height
in the Layout tab after you have clicked on the table. The Table
Design tab allows you to format the table. To do this, select the
appropriate settings in the Table Style Options section and a
suitable table style. Each table style contains its own settings for the
font design. You can manually adjust these settings as well as the
formatting of the table after you have selected the most suitable
table style.
Please design the tables in your report as uniformly as possible,
considering different purposes (e.g., literature review or
presentation of a data analysis). In addition, each table should be as
clear as possible. For this purpose, make sure that the row height is
sufficiently large, refrain from excessive text formatting and reduce
the font size if necessary. Insert a blank line after each table to
create sufficient space between the table and the following text,
unless the table is followed by a page break.
Each table needs its own caption. To caption a table, click in the
table and then click the “Insert Caption” button, located in the
section Captions of the References tab. In the window that opens,
select “Tab.” as label and insert a colon and the name of the table
after the numbering. If the label “Tab.” is not available – which
may be the case the first time you label a new table – click the
“New Label” button, then enter “Tab.” (without the quotation
marks but including the period), set the position of the caption to
“Above selected item,” and confirm your entry. If the numbering
does not include the chapter number, activate the corresponding
function by clicking on the “Numbering...” button. In the following
window, you can activate the option “Include chapter number” and
select “Heading 1” as the style the chapter starts with and
“. (period)” as the separator.
In addition to the caption, each table, such as Tab. 2.1, should be
cross-referenced in the text. To create a cross-reference, click the
button of the same name in the section Links in the Insert tab or in
the section Captions in the References tab. Select “Tab.” as the
reference type and then select the table to be referenced. In the
report text, always refer to “Only label and number” of a table.

Figures
Besides tables, you can use figures to visualize your work. It is best
to create figures yourself in suitable software applications, such as
Microsoft Visio or PowerPoint. When creating figures, make sure to
stay within the available width (15 cm). This allows you to insert
the figures with a scale of 100% and to specify the size of graphical
elements and text in the figures during creation. If possible, use the
same font and size for all text in the figures in your report to create
a consistent look and feel. You may adopt illustrations from other
works if necessary. In this case, try to reproduce the figure in your
preferred software application and indicate the source of the figure
in the figure caption. In exceptional cases, you may also use
screenshots. Please note, however, that screenshots with a
sufficiently high resolution usually increase the storage space
requirements of your report document.
To insert a figure, you can either copy it directly from another
software application into your report, or you can save your figure
temporarily and insert it using the “Insert Pictures” button in the
section Illustrations in the Insert tab. Vector graphic formats such as
“Enhanced Metafile (*.emf)” suit this purpose because they can be
scaled without loss of quality if necessary. After inserting, right-
click on the image and select the Size and Position menu item to
check that the image is at its original size and that the wrapping
style “In line with text” is selected. These settings are also available
in the Picture Format tab, which appears as soon as you click on the
figure.
To label figures, proceed in the same way as for tables, but select
the label “Fig.” instead of “Tab.” (see Fig. 2.1). Please remember to
include a reference in the text for each figure. Inserting a blank line
after a figure is optional.

The bibliography is placed at the end, all other directories at the
beginning of the report in the order listed above. While the table of
content is an integral part of every report, the other indexes are
needed only if they contain at least one entry. Remove directories
you do not need for your report from the template.
Word generates the first three directories automatically when you
use the appropriate styles. Make sure to check and update the
directories again before submitting the report. For this purpose,
right-click in the directory to be updated and then click on “Update
Field”. In the dialog box that opens, select “Update entire table”. If
you have formatted headings and captions correctly, the directories
should include all entries.
The indices of abbreviations and symbols must be created manually.
To do this, insert a new line and use the tab key after the
abbreviation or symbol to be listed, followed by the description of
the abbreviation or symbol. The style for both directories is “Index
of Abbreviations”. Include all abbreviations in the index that are
uncommon or not listed in English dictionaries (e.g., Oxford,
Cambridge, and Merriam-Webster). Abbreviations such as “etc.” or
“e.g.” thus do not belong in the index. If an abbreviation – whether
common or listed in the index of abbreviations – contains a space
(which is unlikely in English), you should insert the space as a
protected space ([Ctrl]+[Shift]+[Space]). This applies both in the
index of abbreviations and in the text. You should introduce all
abbreviations in the index of abbreviations when they first appear
in the text by writing out the description and inserting the
abbreviation in parentheses.
To create the bibliography, you should use an external literature
management software. You can find more information on this in the
next chapter.
Citing
Citation Style
You are obliged to mark other’s ideas as such in your report. If you
do not comply with this obligation or do so insufficiently, your
report will be assessed as plagiarism and thus, as failed. For
formatting your references in the text as well as in the bibliography,
please use the citation style of the American Psychological
Association (APA) in its latest edition. This is currently the APA
Style (7th ed.). This citation style is widely used, including by
leading academic journals in information systems, e.g.,
Management Information Systems Quarterly. All common literature
management software packages include this style, which is
therefore comparatively easy to implement. In addition, you can
find a lot of information on the Internet about the application of
this citation style, as for instance on the corresponding website of
the APA. If your literature management software does not include
the latest edition of the citation style, you can fall back on an older
edition if you do so consistently.
In-Text Citations
Each reference in APA Style (7th ed.) consists of two components: a
citation in the text – including tables, figures, footnotes, and
appendices – and a reference in the bibliography. A citation in the
text is required for both direct and indirect citations and indicates
at least the source’s author(s) and year of publication. We can
differentiate between a citation in parentheses and a narrative
citation. A citation in parentheses includes author(s) and year
separated by a comma after the quote in the text. If the author
name(s) are part of the text, they are simply followed by the year of
publication in parentheses. Tab. 3.1 shows an overview of the
possible formatting of citations in the text.

If your citation refers to a specific passage in the source, you must
additionally specify its location after the year of publication,

but can also refer to entire chapters, tables, figures, etc. For further
explanations and examples on this as well as on special cases of in-
text citations, please visit the APA web pages on in-text citations.
Bibliography
The bibliography of the report must contain all sources cited in the
text. In turn, you must cite all sources listed in the bibliography in
the text. The easiest way to ensure that the bibliography and the
citations in the text match is to use a literature management
software such as Citavi, Zotero, or EndNote.
The APA Style (7th ed.) includes formatting for different types of
sources in the bibliography (e.g., journal articles, books, conference
papers). These formattings are included in most literature
management software packages, which can generate the
bibliography correctly, if you have stored all necessary data. You
should check whether this is the case before submitting the report
and, if necessary, add missing data. If, despite complete and correct
data, some of the references in the bibliography are not formatted
correctly, adjust them manually before submitting the report. If the
formatting style of the bibliography is provided by your reference
management software, please make sure that the text in the
bibliography has a hanging indent of 1.27 cm and that there is no

correspond to the standard text. The “Bibliography” style sheet
